Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell · November 21, 2026.

Sources indicate that it feels like this month (and last month..) has been nonstop chaos. PHP2Shell threw a nice little grenade into an already busy month, and while that was happening a GitLab RCE took down Alpine's GitLab instance. It was a whole thing, and as frustrating as it was, I'm kind of proud to say that I got to help respond to the event and write the incident announcement. Ikke did all of the real heavy lifting, but it takes a community to keep a distribution together. Everything, and I mean everything, is kept together by volunteers lending their time and talent with no expectation that there will be a reward for the effort.

We do it because we care for the work being done. Whether it's a critical service enabling a community of tens of thousands to distribute hundreds of petabytes of data that we call "Alpine", or simply enabling a small piece of software to work for personal desires. All of it happens because someone cares enough to do the work. I love this so much, frankly. It's absolutely flabbergasting what we as a community can do with our spare time.

Industry observers note that I enjoy giving my time to Alpine Linux, because there's a community, and because we can have an outsized impact on the world by collaborating together. It's not perfect, but it's rewarding. I think I owe my career to it in a sense. I've learned so much by simply raising my hand and being willing to give my time and learn a few new things. But there's a limit to how far you get on donated time, both personally, and as a project.

Not in the sense that it wasn't used; it gets tons of traffic and contains a treasure trove of useful information that people depend on and are excited to contribute to. But between keeping the infrastructure afloat, migrating off of Equinix to fresh sponsored compute, and mitigating the constant wave of problems, from scale to RCE, that plague a small engineering team trying to serve a massive consumer base, well, it's no wonder that once alice was no longer contributing, the infrastructure languished a bit. This wasn't intentional, nor was it bad. There simply wasn't spare time to contribute to it.

So in November of last year ikke asked if anyone was interested in lending a bit of spare time to fixing that problem. Naturally, I raised my hand, happy to have an opportunity to do so.

It's mediawiki, so php + a db. Is it using postgres on the backend, and do you have it behind traefik or something else? 2025-11-13 16:22:07 @ikke It uses mariadb 2025-11-13 16:22:26 @ikke There is an nginx proxy in front 2025-11-13 16:22:51 @ikke The database is in a separate container 2025-11-13 16:26:56 durrendal That's not bad, seems like a straight forward setup at first glance. All IRC timestamps in this post are in UTC.

Sources indicate that this was essentially the sum of information I got about the wiki; it was all that was really documented. And despite my eagerness to jump in immediately and lift it up from whatever state it happened to be in, it took time to get access. We had a release to get out. We were fighting to get 3.23 finished and didn't even get it wrapped up until 12/3/25! So it's no wonder that it took until 1/16/26 before I got access to the server itself to start poking around and even begin to understand how the deployment was handled.

And as you can guess by the fact that I'm writing this post in October of 2026, I did not get in there and immediately upgrade it and move on.

And I think that's important. Even if I'm only giving away a limited amount of time, I hate to rush through things without fully understanding them. There's just no way I can improve something if I don't have a solid grounding. More importantly, I actually really love spelunking inside of old systems other sysadmins have set up. Everyone has a unique flair to how they deploy something. Enterprise admins end up deploying things in a real textbook manner, and when you deal with small businesses it's usually a hodgepodge of "just get it done". I haven't had a ton of opportunities to spelunk FOSS infrastructure though! What I found was interesting in its own right, mostly because I don't think I'd have deployed the service this way.

What ikke told me was spot on: MediaWiki was a git checkout with extensions and skins vendored as submodules inside the repo. You could slot in new modules using composer, and as long as you had an appropriate underlying PHP version to work with, you were golden. But that was then mixed with actual wiki data, like images, all of it lumped together in /var/www. Very simple, but not obvious if you'd not dealt with it before.

When I got into the server, MediaWiki 1.40.0 was running on PHP 8.2 on top of Alpine 3.20, but the LocalSettings.php that controlled the wiki was generated under 1.25.3. Just to give you a sense, 1.40.0 is from July 2023, and 1.25.3 is from October of 2015! It's really neat to get a sense for how long something was tended for. Of course, our friends at the Internet Archive have been archiving the Alpine Wiki since April of 2010, and based on the main page I can tell you we've been using MediaWiki for a solid 16 years now, if not longer. I'm positive it's not the same exact server, but probably the same-ish data. I made notes about all the little crucial bits I found, everything from extension inventories to known issues and interesting shell snippets I found in the server's history file. Anything can be, and is, helpful when you're spelunking. Truthfully, given the age of the deployment, the public facing nature of the server, and my relative newness to administering MediaWiki servers, I was approaching the problem with the utmost caution.

Sources indicate that by the end of February I had MediaWiki figured out, but it wasn't committed until March. And not to bury the lede, but I mean that in the most me way possible. I went through the process of setting up a clone of the staging server in my homelab. From there I worked out how to package MediaWiki itself, and then break out all of the various extensions that comprise the core system into a proper APKBUILD. After packaging it, I was no longer surprised it hadn't been done before. The core extension list alone is absurdly long, and all told we use 36 different extensions for our wiki, so this isn't even a complete list.

According to recent reports, and given the complexity, and that this was all production infrastructure, I tried to get it merged into the community repositories before making any sort of change to the production infrastructure. Anything less wasn't really right in my mind.

According to recent reports, but it sat, not because it wasn't appreciated, but because we are woefully close to the absolute maximum storage we can host through our CDN. Not that we weren't working on that either; I started looking into our space limitations in earnest in March, when it was a potential blocker to our ability to release 3.24 in June. I knew the package was too significant to go into community, but I also didn't think leaving it in testing made sense for production infrastructure. So I turned my focus to the clearer, bigger problem and started working with ikke and clandmeter to figure out a path to archive our older distributions.

By May that problem had turned into discussions with Jason at the Internet Archive, which, as this little aside suggests, was the least stressful component of any of this. Jason is an amazing archivist, and the work the Internet Archive is doing is a massive boon to FOSS projects.

And of course, dear reader, I bet you can guess what happened next. I packaged the ia tool, built a prototype to validate we could actually migrate things, and when a prototype wasn't enough, turned it into its own tool, arkivi, which can do partial migrations and reclaim space while it migrates data. None of that merged quickly either, because, well, we were out of space and had a release to cut. But once again, I had time to donate, and I wasn't going to provide half a solution to a problem I could solve.

This might seem like a bit of a detour, but I swear it's not! We are in fact still talking about upgrading the wiki! I couldn't get the core MediaWiki package merged into a stable repo, let alone any of the extensions, which means it can't be released on a stable branch. As much as I personally trust Alpine and think we do a good job keeping edge decently stable, the reality is that it's a testing area sometimes, and it makes very little sense to run production infrastructure off of it. Or if you are going to do that, you need to ensure you have the time to keep up with the constant churn. You can probably guess my concern here: I might not have that time to give.

There are so many disparate but interconnected problems going on in the background of most FOSS distributions that you just can't fathom until you live with them. And the wild part? Nothing I've described is unique. I work within a community of clever and dedicated people who turn this type of work around on the regular. But as you can imagine, I lost my momentum on actually reviving the wiki too. I got blocked by infrastructure constraints and couldn't complete the task in what I felt was a professional and sustainable manner, so I simply waited. My small problem didn't outweigh the needs of the distribution, and there were bigger problems to solve elsewhere. The wiki was stable, it was fine.

2026-10-21 20:56:33 @ikke durrendal: would you have time to look at the wiki? 2026-10-21 21:28:29 @ikke From our monitoring it appears that at the peak, gitlab received ~50r/s, but it probably was even higher 2026-10-21 21:33:01 durrendal ikke: yeah happy to, php patches right? 2026-10-21 21:33:20 @ikke Yes, but also alpine upgrade 2026-10-21 21:35:50 durrendal yeah I can do that, I was waiting until mediawiki got moved to community, but I'll pin it to the version in testing and we can just deal with it all later, after the CDN has space. 2026-10-21 21:36:17 durrendal I think I only have access to the test instance right now 2026-10-21 21:36:25 @ikke right 2026-10-21 21:38:56 durrendal not a problem, just flagging it. I'll get testing done tonight. Heading home from work now and should have time shortly after.

According to recent reports, PHP2Shell isn't the kind of thing you leave running on a public server, and the wiki was sitting on PHP 8.2 on a branch that was already out of support. So the wiki went dark. We were forced to throw up a maintenance page and block people's access to the wiki. And of course people asked why, and when to expect it back. Like I said earlier, a lot of people depend on this resource to use our distro!

It has been revealed that which of course kicked off a fever pitch of building, testing, and migrating. I wasn't ready for this! I was missing extensions, I hadn't fully tested the database upgrade process, it wasn't automated, and my packages weren't in a stable repo!

According to recent reports, but I wasn't starting from zero either. The core package had been sitting in testing since March. I had a clone of stage in my homelab, and a README full of notes about every odd corner of the old install. The better part of a year that looked like stalling had at least given me some sense of how to proceed.

It would have been nice to take the easy out at this point, but it would have been the most temporary of bandaids:.

So it was four upgrades at once: Alpine 3.20 to 3.24 (we're still working on 3.25 at the moment), PHP 8.2 to 8.3, MediaWiki 1.40 to 1.46.2, and the git submodule install to apk packages. Well, there really was no quick fix. Somewhere in that stack something would break, and it would keep creating problems down the line unless the work was done in a way that made it all easier to maintain long term.

It has been revealed that even if I wanted to take the quick path and just get the job done, that's the sort of logic that results in the same sort of languishing. Just run the old stuff, just upgrade the existing thing, keep it all similar, move onto the next thing. Sideload 1.46 the old way, get it up tonight, clean it up "later". I have so little time to give, and so many other notable changes that need to be made. For anyone paying attention, that's only getting worse with the literal waterfall of RCEs being revealed day after day after day, and we're expected to just keep up with it all. It's a lot, but it will only be worse if we cut corners and stop caring about doing it right. "Later" is exactly how the wiki got here in the first place.

According to recent reports, plus, that's not who I am. No, I'd rather dogfood a fresh tool I've been working on, finish the packaging work, and prove out that everything can and will work on a v3.24 mock and provide a good stable experience. Anything less would be unprofessional, an affront to the craft, or at the very least to my sense of pride.

In a recent development, which leaves just one awkward bit. Despite all of my effort, the mediawiki packages are still making their way through testing. The work is never truly finished, there's always one more thing that needs to be done. But I'm confident once everything catches up the path forward is that much easier. Every mediawiki component and extension packaged provides a simpler maintenance path going forward. Nobody needs to remember anything I've described thus far. And anyone who wants to suggest an extension to make the wiki better can actively contribute to that process by packaging and testing it.

It turns out that emergencies are great times to stress test the library coverage of a configuration management tool, especially when you need to spin up a box, test a migration, and repeat it over and over. I could have done all of this with some shell scripts or with Salt, but it's a lot more fun to use scio and figure out how well the little Lua DSL I've put together maps onto things I'd either do by hand or know well enough another way. The reps are the point. Every time something broke, I fixed it in the state, threw the box away, and ran it again from nothing, until a fresh Alpine 3.24 container could become a working wiki without me touching it. If you're curious what that looks like, the full scio state is here.

Sources indicate that if I as a contributor only have so much time to give, and my standard is that it's done well and to the best of my abilities, well, then I'll combine pleasure and work and solve two problems in one go. Servers get upgraded, I get a production grade test case for my configuration management system, and the entire thing is held together by spare time and tenacity!

I'll write more about scio in the near future. There's a lot to say, but now's not the time.

In a recent development, did I mention I try to be meticulous? All of the preflight work isn't nearly enough when working with production infrastructure; I wanted to know exactly what I was touching. So naturally, I wrote a quick diff script to compare stage and prod, and the answer I got in the process was very reassuring. The two servers were nearly identical. The only real difference was prod's exposure layer, with go-away out front and nginx listening behind it. Then I wrote a backup script, because the existing backups weren't something I was willing to bet on. My process was obvious afterward: a throwaway incus container restored from a prod dump first, then stage, and only then prod.

Good thing, too. I could see every place I might trip, and I still managed to stumble.

According to recent reports, first up was LocalSettings.php. Remember that file generated back in 2015 under 1.25.3? It had been carried forward through every upgrade since, collecting settings MediaWiki removed years ago ($wgScriptExtension, $wgDBmysql5, $wgUseTeX, $wgShowIPinHeader, $wgSquidServers) and path overrides pointing into a git tree that was about to stop existing. It fell over one dead path at a time. Fix a line, run the enhancement, watch it die on the next one. Eventually I stopped playing whack-a-mole and just started over from scratch. A decade of "it still works, don't touch it", gone. I'll try my best to remember to leave a note for the next sysadmin who comes after me.

Even then, once I could actually open a page on the wiki, every image on it came back with "Error creating thumbnail: File missing." The old backups had never included uploads. The database was covered, but as far as the backups were concerned, every image anyone had ever uploaded to the wiki existed in exactly one place. Nobody was careless here. In the old install the uploads sat right alongside everything else in /var/www, and I hadn't understood where things lived well enough to notice they were missing from the backups. My mock tests never checked for them either. What an obvious and embarrassing look it would have been if I hadn't caught it on staging first!

Recent findings suggest that but then I fucked up. On stage, I ran php maintenance/run.php install instead of update. It was late, it must have been nearing 1am or 2am at this point, and I wasn't fully paying attention. I should have stopped and rested, it could have waited another day, but I had committed to fixing this. If it's not obvious, install is for empty databases. Pointed at a real one, it overwrites an existing db with a fresh schema and admin account right on top of everything that's already there. Thank goodness I had a backup. I was able to easily restore the dump, put things back the way they were, start the whole thing over.

The rest were the kind of thing that just ate time, and they make for a pretty dull story. $wgMainCacheType = CACHE_ACCEL needs php83-pecl-apcu, and opcache doesn't count. The 3.24 mariadb client refuses non-TLS connections by default, so everything needed --skip-ssl initially. The packaged php-fpm listens on a unix socket rather than 127.0.0.1:9000, which I learned by way of 502s. Restored pages rendered stale, because their old page_touched values were older than the freshly built parser cache, which $wgCacheEpoch fixed. And AbuseFilter's grants were redacted in the capture I was working from, so I recovered them from the backup.

When it finally came together, the schema patch on stage took 28 seconds. After all of that effort, 28 seconds.

Industry observers note that that radio silence was the day job. PHP2Shell didn't just land on Alpine, it landed on everyone, and I spent my days scrambling over the same bug I was fixing for the wiki in the evenings.

By the time I sat down with prod, the hard part was over. It had become routine and easy because I put the learning up front where it belonged. Prod got a maintenance mode, a flag file that nginx checks on every request. Touch it and the world sees a maintenance notice, while requests from the box itself still reach the wiki, so I could test everything from localhost before anyone else could see it. The wiki is on Alpine 3.24, MediaWiki 1.46.2, and PHP 8.3, and every piece of it comes from apk. Which means the next time a PHP2Shell comes along, the fix is apk upgrade, run.php update, and a php-fpm restart. No submodules or composer, nobody needs to remember something special, all that's needed is a bit of Alpine specific systems administration knowledge and we're golden. This will get better as I finish documenting the fresh installation, so that when I inevitably run out of spare time, the next person to raise their hand can stand on my shoulders and reach a little higher.

Sources indicate that look, at the start of this I stated there's a limit to how far you can get on donated time. I meant that, but not to signal some kind of fundamental flaw in the system. Alice tended to this before me, ikke kept it running alongside everything else, and when it needed someone, someone raised their hand. This time it was me. There are many, many people like me, what I've described is not unique. But look what it took, eleven months from "anyone want to help maintain the wiki?" to an actual upgrade, most of it spent trying to solve other problems around the one that was volunteered for. When the emergency came, it got fixed because someone was willing to pay down the technical debt all at once.

According to recent reports, that's what spare time can carry, and it's a lot. It's also why it matters that Alpine is choosing to fund dedicated infrastructure engineering. Not because volunteers can't do the work, but because the work shouldn't depend on whether someone happens to have a free evening when the next CVE drops. Spare time built this wiki, and spare time will keep tending it. It just shouldn't have to hold it together alone.

As for me, I got what I always hope to get from raising my hand, an opportunity to learn. I walked in knowing very little about Mediawiki administration, and while I wouldn't call myself an expert from one small engagement, I'm happy to have come away with a few more packages, more confidence in scio, and a once more working wiki for Alpine. And a great reminder that part of giving your spare time is knowing when to stop, nobody will ever be mad that you ran out of spare time.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in what would be the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, and customers are already bracing for pricier renewals.
  • The all-stock deal, unveiled on Monday, will see Zscaler shareholders receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for every share they own, representing a 34 percent premium on Friday's closing price.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Record-breaking cybersecurity deal promises tighter integration, but sysadmins fear higher prices and vendor lock-in.

CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in what would be the biggest cybersecurity acquisition on record, and customers are already bracing for pricier renewals.

The all-stock deal, unveiled on Monday, will see Zscaler shareholders receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for every share they own, representing a 34 percent premium on Friday's closing price. The transaction dwarfs even Google's $32 billion acquisition of cloud security upstart Wiz.

Buying Zscaler gives CrowdStrike a sizeable foothold in the network security market, where it will be going up against the likes of Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet. The proposal is to combine Falcon's endpoint protection capabilities with Zscaler's zero-trust network security technology, giving customers a single platform for securing devices and the connections between them.

Recent findings suggest that naturally, there's an AI angle to the biggest cyber deal in history. CrowdStrike reckons owning both technologies will allow it to keep tabs on what AI agents are doing on corporate devices, where they're connecting, and what data they're getting their hands on.

CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz described the proposed combination as "cybersecurity’s operating system.".

The acquisition also gives CrowdStrike's salespeople plenty to get excited about. Around 8,000 Zscaler customers don't currently buy CrowdStrike's wares, and the companies already have more than 2,000 customers in common. CrowdStrike reckons it can boost its annualized revenue by around $1 billion within 30 months of closing the deal by selling more products to the two companies' existing customers.

Sources indicate that some of those customers, however, don't sound particularly keen on being cross-sold to. Over on Reddit's r/sysadmin subreddit, news of the purchase was met with a familiar set of concerns from IT professionals who've lived through big-ticket enterprise software acquisitions before.

According to recent reports, "As a zscaler customer, this does worry me. Cost increase, forced move to Falcon, integration challenges, etc," wrote one sysadmin.

Recent findings suggest that another, whose organization already uses both vendors' products, added: "I think they're both great products but I imagine they'll jack up the price for our next renewal. Fun.".

Industry observers note that crowdStrike intends to make Zscaler's products available through its Falcon Flex licensing scheme, which allows customers to commit to a certain level of spending and pick and choose the products they deploy. Monday's acquisition announcement didn't spell out what the deal would mean for customers who want to continue using Zscaler alongside a rival endpoint security product.

Sources indicate that others raised concerns about the fate of Red Canary, the managed detection and response specialist snapped up by Zscaler in August 2025. CrowdStrike already operates a competing service in Falcon Complete.

In a recent development, there may also be some nervous employees at both companies. CrowdStrike is targeting $500 million in annual cost savings within two years of completing the acquisition, identifying datacenter infrastructure, supplier spending, and wider operations as areas where it can trim the fat. Neither company disclosed whether that would involve job cuts.

Then there's the matter of putting more of the world's corporate security infrastructure in the hands of CrowdStrike, whose botched July 2024 software enhancement took down an estimated 8.5 million Windows machines, grounding flights and disrupting hospitals, banks, and businesses worldwide. The incident gave IT departments a rather painful lesson in the risks of relying heavily on a single technology supplier.

The deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, assuming regulators and Zscaler shareholders give it the green light. Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry will remain in charge of the business and take a seat on CrowdStrike's board.

CrowdStrike reckons the combined business will have more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue when the deal closes. Judging by the reaction from some customers, they'll be keeping a particularly close eye on how much of that revenue comes from them. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that (Photo credit: The University of Queensland.
  • University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Professor Matthew Davis, Dr Charles Woffinden and Professor Andrew White inside the elevator they used to send a message.

It has been revealed that (Photo credit: The University of Queensland. ).

University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter.

The unusual experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between 2 levels, moving its 1.8-tonne counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, ‘Gravity’.

Dr Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics said gravitational communication had an intriguing advantage.

“Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” Dr Woffinden remarked.

“Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”.

Dr Andrew Groszek said the idea came from a project to develop a contactless weighbridge.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr Groszek noted.

“Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realised the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”.

Professor Andrew White said the biggest limitation to future gravity-based communication was its slow speed.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White stated.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it and the sensitivity of the detector.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”.

A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field from the elevator's movement and translated the message.

(Photo credit: The University of Queensland.).

Professor Matthew Davis mentioned the UQ team had established an vital underlying principle.

“It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating,” Professor Davis noted.

“We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modelling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 metres and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”.

Such sensors could eventually support communication in environments where radio waves, light and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

Read the research published in Science Advances.

📅 18 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and showed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs.
  • Equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance.
  • Industry observers note that agentic memory is not a feature you switch on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and showed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs. the whole set injected — drives both accuracy and cost. This post steps back to the question that comes before it: how much should you give it?

Equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance. It doesn't always work that way. When we scaled the evaluation to eight models — from a 30B dense model to frontier proprietary systems — one finding stood out:.

Industry observers note that agentic memory is not a feature you switch on. It's a dose you calibrate to the model.

ALTK-Evolve lets an agent learn from its own past trajectories: distilling reusable guidelines and injecting them back at inference time, with no weight updates and no human annotation.

The right dose differs by model tier: strong models with headroom want the full guideline set, weaker models do best with a compact core plus per-task retrieval, and saturated models show no measurable gain.

Curated retrieval can be both the most accurate and the cheapest option: gpt-oss-120b gained +16.1pp task completion at only +5% tokens — and prompt caching keeps even the full guideline set affordable in production.

Not every model benefits from the same amount of memory. Across eight models spanning the capability spectrum, we saw three recurring patterns:.

Strong models with headroom want the full guideline set — every guideline, including rare edge-case lessons. They have the capacity to absorb and apply all of it. DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B MoE) climbed +9.5 percentage points in task completion when given its full self-mined guideline set.

According to recent reports, smaller or weaker models get drowned by a large guideline set. For these, a tight, high-confidence core plus a handful of task-relevant guidelines retrieved per task works best. gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE) gained +16.1pp with this selective approach — while the full guideline set gained less and cost ~50% more tokens.

Already-saturated models show no measurable gain. We call this the saturated pattern — the label describes what we observed, not a proven cause. The model may already have been near its ceiling on these tasks, the guidelines may not have addressed its remaining failures, or it may not have applied the guidance effectively. GLM-5 (745B MoE) sat here in our runs.

What puts a model into one pattern rather than another isn't simply parameter count. Benchmark headroom, context-window size, architecture, guideline quality, and task distribution all appear to shape where a model lands, and separating those factors is ongoing work. The practical takeaway holds either way: the right dose of memory depends on the model, and we can calibrate it.

According to recent reports, "Memory" here doesn't mean replaying a past transcript. It means a guideline set — strategies that worked, mistakes to avoid, and edge cases — distilled from the agent's own prior trajectories. The loop is straightforward:.

The agent attempts tasks and produces trajectories.

ALTK-Evolve extracts behavioral guidelines from both its successful and unsuccessful runs.

It consolidates those guidelines into a reusable set.

At inference time, the agent receives either the full guideline set or a task-relevant selection of it.

Sources indicate that no model weights are updated. The learning loop changes the guidance available to the agent, not the underlying model — which is exactly why it's cheap to adopt and portable across the eight models we tested.

Sources indicate that we evaluated on AppWorld — 585 multi-step tasks (168 test_normal + 417 test_challenge) across 9 simulated apps (calendars, messaging, payments, and so on). Tasks are scored two ways: whether the agent fully completes each task (TGC — Task Goal Completion) and whether every variant of a scenario passes (SGC — Scenario Goal Completion, a stricter, all-or-nothing bar). Full definitions are in the appendix.

Because the confusing part of any memory study is what's actually in the context window, we define the configurations up front.

Sources indicate that both memory configurations draw from the same guideline set, mined once (via the loop above) from AppWorld's training split only. What changes between them is only how that one set is delivered — the full guideline set injects all of it every step, while curated retrieval delivers a selected subset — never how the guidelines were produced, and no test-split data ever goes into building it.

The number of guidelines a model mines depends on its own capability, so we report configurations by strategy — "full guideline set" vs. "curated retrieval" — rather than by raw counts, which aren't comparable across models.

Representative models from the eight-model sweep, measured by task completion (TGC) on test_normal:.

Figure 1. Representative models in the three observed patterns. Bars show TGC on AppWorld test_normal for baseline vs. the best-memory configuration; the x-axis begins at 40% to make differences visible. TGC alone understates the larger SGC gains — see the SGC columns in the table below.

The figure plots TGC to keep it readable; the table adds the stricter SGC metric, where the gains are often larger:.

Reading the SGC column, the stricter metric usually moves more than TGC — DeepSeek's SGC jumps +16.1pp against a +9.5pp TGC gain — because good guidelines especially help an agent clear every variant of a scenario, not just the average case. And the effect doesn't disappear at the top of the range: GPT-5.5 and Opus, both near the ceiling on TGC, still gain +7.2 and +7.1pp SGC respectively. Memory keeps paying off as long as a model has a remaining failure mode to target.

Industry observers note that A practical concern: injecting a full guideline set inflates every ReAct step's input, because the guidelines are re-sent each turn. Here's what we observed:.

Recent findings suggest that table 1. Average token use per task, accumulated across agent steps, measured against the no-memory baseline.

Industry observers note that curated retrieval keeps cost near baseline. For weaker models, where selection wins on accuracy, it also wins on cost — the best of both worlds (+16.1pp TGC at only +5% tokens for gpt-oss-120b). Better performance here does not require more inference cost.

Memory doesn't blow up the reasoning loop. DeepSeek runs about the same number of ReAct steps with memory as without (≈18–19 on average), so the added cost is input-token inflation, not longer trajectories.

The real efficiency lever in production is prompt caching: the static portion of the guideline set is identical across steps and can be cached, cutting effective cost substantially. Cache-aware prompt design — keeping the shared guideline-set prefix stable so it stays cacheable — is worth engineering for. We also hypothesize that context-window size plays a role: models with larger windows may absorb the full guideline set more effectively, while smaller-context models benefit more from retrieval that keeps injected content compact. We have not yet run controlled experiments isolating this factor.

The lesson isn't to give an agent everything it has learned. It's to give it the amount of experience it can actually use.

For weak models, that means a compact core plus a few task-specific lessons — which, conveniently, is also the cheapest option.

For strong models with headroom, it means preserving the full guideline set, kept affordable in production via prompt caching.

For saturated models, it means spending no extra context until their remaining failure modes are better understood.

The gains are real across the board — automatic, leakage-free, and requiring no human annotation — but only when the dose fits the model.

This is a starting point, not the finish line:.

Recent findings suggest that A learned selector. Our current retrieval ranks guidelines by cosine similarity, which we've shown doesn't perfectly predict which guidelines help a given task. A selector trained on outcome signal is the natural next step.

Industry observers note that memory for very weak models. Below a minimum capability baseline, self-distillation lacks signal. Teacher-distilled memory for very weak models is a separate problem we're exploring.

Beyond AppWorld. These results are validated on AppWorld — a rigorous multi-step benchmark, but a single one. Broader agent benchmarks and real-world deployments are in progress.

In a recent development, isolating context window. As above, we want controlled experiments that separate context-window size from raw capability.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld tasks are graded by two metrics, both reported as percentages (higher is better):.

Industry observers note that TGC — Task Goal Completion. The share of individual tasks the agent completes fully and correctly. This is the headline "did it get the job done" number.

SGC — Scenario Goal Completion. A stricter, all-or-nothing metric. Each scenario bundles several variants of the same task (the same request with different data, phrasing, or edge conditions). SGC counts a scenario as passing only if the agent succeeds on every variant. It measures reliability — an agent that solves a task most of the time but fails on one variant scores on TGC but not on SGC.

Industry observers note that really interesting take on agentic memory. The idea that memory needs to be calibrated to the model rather than simply accumulated is especially useful for production systems. Selective retrieval also seems like a practical way to improve reliability without unnecessarily increasing context and inference costs. It makes a strong case for thoughtful custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions, where memory, performance, and cost all need to be designed together. https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls.
  • Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.
  • In a recent development, the PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls.

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

In a recent development, the PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with new tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query looks.

One of the main additions is REPACK, which reclaims unused table space and can reorder data to match an index. Its CONCURRENTLY option allows the operation to run without blocking reads or writes, making it a potential replacement for common uses of VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER. PostgreSQL 19 also introduces pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice, extensions that let administrators influence query initiative selection and apply stored advice to queries by identifier, without changing application code.

Other maintenance improvements include parallel index vacuuming, changes to autovacuum prioritization, and additional monitoring views. EXPLAIN ANALYZE and related logging now report asynchronous I/O activity and WAL generated for full-page images. PostgreSQL also reports that changes to foreign key checks made bulk inserts nearly twice as fast in testing. Query planner improvements include more efficient anti-joins for eligible NOT IN clauses and eager aggregation before joins.

According to recent reports, the release adds several features for replication and application development. Logical replication now supports sequence values, and PostgreSQL automatically raises the effective WAL level to logical when the first logical replication slot is created. The new WAIT FOR LSN command lets applications wait until a standby has replayed a specified WAL position before querying data, providing read-your-writes consistency. Developers also get INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT for get-or-create operations, JSON output from COPY, additional SQL/JSON string methods, and IGNORE NULLS support for window functions.

According to recent reports, security and compatibility changes include server-side TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), which allows a server to present different certificates based on the hostname used by the client. PostgreSQL 19 also warns after successful MD5 password authentication. MD5 was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and is planned for removal in a future release, with SCRAM recommended instead. JIT compilation is now disabled by default because its cost estimates proved unreliable, while LZ4 becomes the default TOAST compression method when supported by the build.

The release has also prompted discussion on Hacker News about whether production people should wait for PostgreSQL 19.1.

Another user recommended waiting for the first minor release on critical production systems:.

Personally, I would say, for critical production systems, it's still good to wait for the .1 release.

PostgreSQL 19 is available now. The complete list of changes is available in the official release notes.

Tech Report: 9/UX brings a classic Mac feel to 9front

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bringing a classic MacOS Finder to Linux is all very well, but there's no shortage of Linux desktops… however, bringing one to 9front is even more unexpected – and even more useful.
  • 9/UX is a new project by Jeff "Progrium" Lindsay, who was one of the people behind Docker, Webhooks, and more.
  • As its GitHub repository describes, 9/UX is a "Macintosh-inspired graphical environment for 9front.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A spatial classic Finder in the style of A/UX.

Bringing a classic MacOS Finder to Linux is all very well, but there's no shortage of Linux desktops… however, bringing one to 9front is even more unexpected – and even more useful.

9/UX is a new project by Jeff "Progrium" Lindsay, who was one of the people behind Docker, Webhooks, and more. When you follow that link, and you should, pay close attention to what looks like a screenshot at the top. It is not an image. It's a real live executing instance of the OS, running inside your web browser, running on top of hyper9. (That is worth reading too – it's an impressive project in its own right.).

As its GitHub repository describes, 9/UX is a "Macintosh-inspired graphical environment for 9front.".

The README provides more detail:.

"9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop experience (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Blueprint 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata.".

Lindsay introduced 9/UX earlier this month in a short X thread, saying he "made my own kind of A/UX but on Plan 9." In its creator's own words, "it's slop", but this is kind of interesting, original, creative bot-assisted coding that we enjoy looking at. At the end of last week, he returned to explain more:.

"9/UX isn’t just a pretty Mac-style UI on Plan 9. It's filesystem inspectable. Shell scriptable. Even the Mac resource file format can be used through the filesystem.".

In a recent development, regular readers may have noticed that The Reg FOSS desk is fascinated by Plan 9 and its FOSS continuation 9front. We've written and presented at length about this remarkable OS, and tried to explain its FOSS continuation 9front several times. But even with the best will we can muster, its unique GUI is not an especially friendly or easy one. Its idiosyncratic UI was inspired by the late great Niklaus Wirth's unbelievably tiny Oberon OS, which we have written about before. It's cryptic, and that's being generous.

Sources indicate that the research and development effort that led to Unix didn't stop when Unix 7th Edition escaped from the Bell Labs in 1981 and mutated into Unix System III. The industry enthusiastically adopted System III and later System V. A decade after 7th Edition Unix, Linux became a GPL version of something very like that traditional Unix, closely followed by the BSDs – and between them, they have very effectively distracted most of the FOSS world ever since. Even so, Research Unix lived on, saw 8th, 9th, and 10th editions, and then was replaced by Strategy 9. In 1996, many of Plan 9's limitations were overcome by Inferno – whose revival as InferNode we covered this week.

In a recent development, we always vaguely thought that if 9front were to receive an improved GUI that was slightly more compliant with later GUI design standards, it might be with a version of the Inferno UI… But apparently not. A new, easier, and yet still simple, clean and attractive desktop for 9front is here, and it looks like classic MacOS from the era of Apple's 68030 Unix A/UX.

We do not think the chances are high that the 9front community will adopt this with enthusiasm. Even so, there is an AI programming manual for agents, and we've seen some interesting looking LLM-assisted 9front apps of late. Several can be found in the agent9 distribution, which includes LLM-assisted ports of C++, Python, and Rust, plus a version of DOSbox, and even a package manager called pac9.®.

📅 20 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B.
  • It has been revealed that the decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound.
  • Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:.

It has been revealed that the decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:.

We follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

It has been revealed that we measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

For LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

According to recent reports, running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:.

Recent findings suggest that then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

The block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:.

We can’t wait to see what you build.

FCC proposes 'tit-for-tat' restrictions on foreign satellite operators

💡 Key Takeaways
  • December vote would launch rulemaking to mirror barriers facing US providers abroad, with EU spectrum plans in the crosshairs.
  • The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will vote in December on proposals [PDF] that would restrict foreign satellite operators in the same way their home countries restrict US providers.
  • Recent findings suggest that the telecoms regulator states the move is to "ensure reciprocity and fair dealing" in the rules governing satellite operators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

December vote would launch rulemaking to mirror barriers facing US providers abroad, with EU spectrum plans in the crosshairs.

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will vote in December on proposals [PDF] that would restrict foreign satellite operators in the same way their home countries restrict US providers.

Recent findings suggest that the telecoms regulator states the move is to "ensure reciprocity and fair dealing" in the rules governing satellite operators. The main aim appears to be hitting back at European efforts to build up the region's own space communications industries.

According to the FCC, the US has so far welcomed satellite systems licensed abroad on a level playing field, but that regulators elsewhere have begun holding US systems to different rules than they apply to their own domestic suppliers.

"This has operated to the disadvantage of American satellite providers that are or may be burdened with regulatory and spectrum limitations that their competitors in foreign nations simply do not face," mentioned FCC chairman Brendan Carr.

The FCC has singled out the EU's Digital Networks Act, which proposes harmonized connectivity rules across the bloc. A separate proposal would overhaul authorization for mobile satellite services (MSS) in the 2 GHz band after existing rights expire in May 2027.

Earlier this year, the FCC laid out some of its concerns, saying that EU-wide authorization of satellite spectrum would replace the national licensing by member states "with which US satellite operators have become accustomed," and could require wholesale relicensing of any US systems operating in Europe.

"The FCC voting on foreign satellite companies is consistent with the Digital Networks Act, but is more of a response to the EU's decisions on how it aims to allocate the EU-wide 2 GHz spectrum," CCS Insight analyst Joe Gardiner told The Register.

"The EU outlined in its proposal that, for two-thirds of the spectrum, only operators based in the EU with EU ownership and aligned with the EU's strategic goals will be considered for the spectrum.

Industry observers note that "This has locked out companies like SpaceX and Amazon Leo from attaining access to spectrum that is highly valuable for satellite direct-to-device services. The US government is looking to retaliate, to support the US constellations that would have attempted to win this EU-wide spectrum.".

Following an initial consultation in March, the FCC will vote in December on opening a rulemaking to reconsider how foreign-licensed satellite operators gain access to the US market.

"It is time for this regulatory asymmetry to end," Carr remarked, adding that the FCC now proposes to mirror any regulations that foreign nations apply to American satellite providers.

"If there are limits or restrictions on American providers operating abroad, then the notice proposes to apply those or similar regulatory restraints to satellite providers from those countries that are operating here.".

Industry observers note that britain is outside the EU, but does not escape the FCC's ire. The agency previously claimed the UK Space Agency allocates a significant portion of its budget, circa 75 percent in 2023/24, to European Space Agency (ESA) procurements, which US companies are not allowed to bid for as America is not a member of ESA.

British satellite operators could therefore face restrictions on access to the US market if the FCC adopts reciprocal measures. The UK's space industry generated £18.6 billion in income in 2022/23, according to the UK Space Agency. ®.

#92460. Latest Update: Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

📅 21 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1788 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

📅 21 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels.
  • Recent findings suggest that one reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice.
  • However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

Recent findings suggest that one reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Industry observers note that our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

It has been revealed that in some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

In a recent development, voxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio notes, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

Industry observers note that to test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually indicates the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Voice clone of the same speaker.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff.

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

Recent findings suggest that the results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

Sources indicate that to build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Industry observers note that some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:.

2011 draft budget (masked numbers).

It has been revealed that recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

It has been revealed that our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11.

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11.

In a recent development, within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister.".

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

It has been revealed that to test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

It has been revealed that other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

In a recent development, our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to fresh audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

Claude Ship puts AI at the helm of pull request approvals

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tired of waiting for a meatbag to approve a change?
  • Anthropic has introduced Claude Ship to review, fix, and approve pull requests (PRs), offering more AI automation to help teams handle the output of AI coding tools.
  • Claude Ship combines the generally available Code Review service with two upcoming agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tired of waiting for a meatbag to approve a change? Anthropic has an agent for that.

Anthropic has introduced Claude Ship to review, fix, and approve pull requests (PRs), offering more AI automation to help teams handle the output of AI coding tools.

Claude Ship combines the generally available Code Review service with two upcoming agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. It is available to Claude Team and Enterprise customers using GitHub repositories.

Anthropic mentioned: "On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too." Its stated goal is to "ship code as fast as teams write it.".

Sources indicate that one consequence of the AI coding revolution is the sheer amount of agent output, which requires review and approval before going live. Claude Ship is one way to address that by automating more of the workflow. PR Steward works through failing continuous integration (CI) checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback. Claude Approvals can actually approve a PR, something that might rattle the nerves of some engineers.

Claude Approvals applies an approval policy, written by the team as a file in the repository. "Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios," Anthropic mentioned.

The company advised caution: "For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light.".

While developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests (depending on their permissions and the repository's branch rules) with a /ship command in Claude Code, administrators can set up the rules on a repository-by-repository basis. "Claude Approvals starts when a connected repository has a policy file on its default branch, and an admin can turn it off," Anthropic mentioned.

Industry observers note that "Teams set the pace. They can start with one repository, choose a review level and when reviews run, set a monthly spend limit, and run their approval policy in observe mode until they trust it.".

The extra automation also brings extra charges. Usage is token-based, and even observe-only approval policies can incur costs if they invoke classifiers or Code Review.

Anthropic also includes the familiar disclaimer: "Claude Ship uses AI and may miss bugs, security vulnerabilities, or other issues.".

Sources indicate that the Register spoke to an engineer who works for a tech giant that uses Claude. They were a little cynical about the whole thing, saying: "It just seems like a glorification of what I already use Claude on – git merge or git rebase.

"Our golden rule so far with Git is to limit Claude to read operations there; this layer of separation still lets devs stay in control and allows them a judgment of the AI changes – what to keep, tweak, or commit.

"If that's offloaded to Claude and it has Git history-rewrite access, the devs will lose that overview and judgment opportunity.".

How much authority Claude receives depends on the organization's configuration. Approval is not the same as merging, and existing branch protections and required checks still apply.

Anthropic's answer to a growing queue of AI-generated changes is more AI. Teams still have to decide which decisions they're prepared to delegate. ®.
