But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go complications for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has noted he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := latest(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture.
  • Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.
  • It has been revealed that agoda has introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries without rewriting the existing service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture.

Nov 23, 2026 2 min read.

It has been revealed that agoda has introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries without rewriting the existing service. The approach combines component-based code organization, automated architecture checks, and incremental migration. The team reported 64% shorter median code review time and 34% shorter time to initial substantive feedback for framework-backed changes compared with legacy code.

It has been revealed that the change addresses growing maintenance challenges in BAPI, which coordinates cancellations, booking amendments, refunds, and customer communications. Agoda extracted the API from its aging core monolith in 2019 through a largely line-by-line migration. As development increased, merge requests more than quadrupled between 2022 and 2025, while some files exceeded 4,000 lines.

In a recent development, the team characterized the migration as a tactical design trade-off, drawing on John K. Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design,.

We had deliberately traded a strategic design approach for a tactical one to prioritize speed to market. This tactical mindset was exactly what the business needed at the time.

Rather than undertake a complete rewrite, the team introduced architectural boundaries incrementally.

The framework, called Platform, organizes code around business domains such as cancellations, rebooking, and payments rather than technical layers. Each component encapsulates its business logic and data access behind defined interfaces, with application, service, repository, and model layers contained within the component. This package-by-component approach aims to localize changes and reduce dependencies between business domains.

Platform framework boundaries inside a domain module (Source: Agoda Blog Post).

Sources indicate that agoda uses the Data Mapper pattern to keep repository-specific models, including database entities and API payloads, out of business logic. Typed builders centralize object creation and transformations, making it easier for developers to find where domain objects and service inputs are constructed.

According to recent reports, the team also uses ArchUnit to encode architectural constraints as automated tests in continuous integration. For example, repository-specific models can only be accessed by their respective repositories. Violations fail the build rather than relying on code reviewers to identify unauthorized dependencies manually.

Sources indicate that the team described these constraints as architectural fitness functions, a concept discussed by Neal Ford and Mark Richards in Software Architecture: The Hard Parts. One engineer explained:.

By codifying our layer boundaries into an ArchUnit test suite, our CI pipeline serves as an automated guardrail, catching structural drift on every pull request before a human reviewer ever sees it.

Platform is now the default for upcoming modules, while existing functionality is migrated incrementally when feature development provides an opportunity.

Recent findings suggest that agoda compared framework-backed and legacy merge requests in Q2 2026. Median review completion time was 1.08 hours for framework-backed changes, compared with 3.02 hours for legacy changes. Time to first substantive feedback was 10.34 hours versus 15.77 hours. Between June and August, framework-backed changes also used 29% fewer AI prompts per 100 changed lines, although median prompts per merge request were similar (20 vs. 22). Agoda cautioned that the AI findings were directional due to the short observation period. A related approach is Spring Modulith, which provides module verification and dependency-cycle checks for Spring Boot applications.

#92433. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1578 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

According to recent reports, that is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

Industry observers note that funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

Sources indicate that that one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

It has been revealed that from there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the latest one.

Recent findings suggest that with funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

According to recent reports, recall returns the original text, not a summary, and highlights exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three notable properties:.

Sources indicate that the agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

According to recent reports, the bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

Recent findings suggest that recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

In a recent development, or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

Recent findings suggest that funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

Industry observers note that A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Sources indicate that claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

Sources indicate that published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

Sources indicate that A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

According to recent reports, the lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

Industry observers note that your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

Industry observers note that funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Sources indicate that full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance.
  • Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own.
  • Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:.

In a recent development, we will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:.

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

In a recent development, IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

Industry observers note that for the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:.

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:.

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:.

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:.

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:.

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:.

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:.

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:.

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:.

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:.

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

#92431. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1552 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • Sources indicate that we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

Sources indicate that we fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

Sources indicate that neoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

Industry observers note that we pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

Recent findings suggest that one NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

Industry observers note that we report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

In a recent development, viDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

It has been revealed that we tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Customers can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

It has been revealed that before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding upcoming documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

Recent findings suggest that so we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

According to recent reports, we provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers at the moment supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Industry observers note that visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

Industry observers note that neoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.
  • At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the manufacturer's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents.

Nov 23, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam, senior software engineer at Netflix, described how the manufacturer's Commerce team retrofitted its software development lifecycle so that AI coding agents and engineers could ship together safely.

Khuzam argued that most of the work was not about agents at all, but about documentation, consistency and review.

Much of Commerce runs as server-driven UI, an approach Netflix has discussed at QCon before. A single screen-composition service behind the API gateway builds screens for iOS, Android, web and TV.

Khuzam opened with a mock tech giant email announcing that every engineer now had Claude Code and asking how much faster everyone was shipping. The problem the team ran into next was summed up in one line.

The team's first attempt was having an agent migrate tests, and it took four tries. The team started with "migrate this file," then added instructions, then the APIs to use, then how to mock data.

Sources indicate that the docs were also hard to find, since the agent's context window ran out before it found the right page. And they were inconsistent, because tests were not written the same way across the codebase.

Developers rated the internal framework at a Net Promoter Score of -3. Moving from one test to a whole feature, from screen to data to route to test, meant teaching the agent how the team builds.

Khuzam described the fix as context engineering, "getting what engineers know into what agents see." The team wrote 45 architecture decision records, each "written for people and for agents.".

According to recent reports, each record covers the context, the decision, a pattern and an anti-pattern, and AI usage notes on what an agent should do. It also links to related docs and code, and the records now ship inside almost every repository.

To keep those records and more than 300 other documents findable, the team borrowed from how search engines read a site. An AGENTS.md file, the project instructions file that coding agents read before anything else, plays the part of robots.txt.

The second half of the talk followed code after an agent writes it. Khuzam noted that the CI pipeline is still deterministic, running builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries.

What changed is how agents plug into each phase. A review agent pre-reviews each pull request against the docs and ADRs, flags anti-patterns and looks at what depends on the change.

Its first version left 23 comments on a single PR, starting with "Overall this PR looks great!" It now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix and the ADR rule it breaks. Engineers can add a revise label to have an agent read the review and push a fix to the same PR. Changes aren't yet auto-merged, and engineers own the code.

Sources indicate that khuzam reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and 32% more pull requests year over year. Developer NPS rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.

Ahead of the session, Khuzam framed the stakes on LinkedIn: "Agents can write code, but what gives us the confidence to ship Tier 0 services to 300M+ members without everything falling apart?".

According to recent reports, work that crosses services raised a harder question. A product engineer building one feature touches the payment API, billing, the gateway and every client, so the team had to decide who owns the context and how it follows the work.

Recent findings suggest that khuzam listed approaches that did not hold up. Loading every repository did not fit, Git submodules were brittle, a Git MCP server "sees one file, not the system," and shared copies went stale.

The team needed context that was accurate, portable across agents, owned per domain and kept fresh. It settled on GraphRAG per domain, taking structure from the code and meaning from the docs and ADRs.

Sources indicate that each graph is pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot and CI review all query the same graph, and every answer cites a file and a line.

It has been revealed that khuzam closed with three rules: decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters. "None of this is upcoming. It's good engineering, built for a new reader.".

Developers interested in learning more can watch InfoQ in the coming weeks for video of the session and can view the session details here.

#92429. Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1434 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Signal ↗ Open Full Page

Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1434 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Signal

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.
  • This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.
  • We’ve already had to do this once with Windows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meredith Whittaker on 20 Nov 2026.

Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default.1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen.2.

In a recent development, the problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

According to recent reports, in order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

Sources indicate that the net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android.2.

People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

According to recent reports, we want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are presently unable to implement these protections on macOS.3.

We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.

We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:.

It has been revealed that we also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that people are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.

In addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across the ecosystem to make the stakes clear. There is a lot of work to be done in the industry to improve the ways that AI agents operate in the operating system, and how and whether they capture and process private data. We are cautiously optimistic that some major OS providers, like Google and Apple, are engaging with us on how these systems should better interface with privacy-sensitive apps like Signal. We hope to have more to share on this topic soon, and that these companies recognize the danger to the ecosystem and work with us and others to create standardized approaches that meaningfully protect privacy across the industry.

Industry observers note that finally, we want to acknowledge that we are not the only ones recognizing these perils, and we are grateful to our allies for pushing for similar changes. We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.

Sources indicate that signal Technology Foundation is the nonprofit home of the Signal app, which is trusted by millions around the world. We protect free expression and enable secure global communication through open source privacy technology. Signal Technology Foundation is a US 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization.

According to recent reports, microsoft Recall captures your screen every few seconds, extracts text from screenshots via optical character recognition, then populates a searchable on-device database with this personal data in order to allow the AI system to query it – potentially exposing and retaining your Signal data indefinitely, including disappearing messages. ↩.

There are multiple versions of Android beyond the Google-provided distributions on Pixel devices. For many vendors, we don’t have a reliable way to detect when a screenshot was attempted if screenshots are already disabled. Rather than choose a poor user experience (where screenshots simply stop working, confusing users), we decided to instead focus on detecting when an AI assistant attempts to access the screen. We automatically enable the “Screen security” setting in Signal Android when this type of access is detected. ↩ ↩2.

Careful readers will note that in addition to not being able to cover all Android devices, we are also not blocking Siri AI on macOS. This is because we cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS. Faced with a lack of clearly documented APIs that allow us to implement screenshot protection, we do not have the tools available that let us do the job. While protections against continuous screen capture exist on macOS, we cannot apply them to screenshots (which is how most agentic systems access data from applications like Signal). Trying to implement screenshot blocking on macOS has revealed to us a minefield of bewildering decisions that place user privacy at risk, including APIs that have been deprecated in favor of screen-protection solutions that only work for streaming media and other DRM-protected content. This is something we hope Apple remedies urgently. For now, the only recommendation we have for macOS 27 consumers is to add Signal to the Excluded Apps section in System Settings > Siri to protect message content from proactive access by Siri AI. ↩.

Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui.
  • Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes.
  • You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

You can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

According to recent reports, in Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

Industry observers note that that same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

There's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

Recent findings suggest that the drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

Industry observers note that this is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

According to recent reports, background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Recent findings suggest that canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

In a recent development, there are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

In a recent development, the image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

According to recent reports, so far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:.

Recent findings suggest that zeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

It has been revealed that this isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

It has been revealed that the same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node indicates up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:.

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

In a recent development, AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:.

According to recent reports, bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

If you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Industry observers note that whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes.

According to recent reports, analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?
