#92427. Async GRPO with LoRA across HF Jobs: a bucket, a proxy, and no NCCL

📅 10 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4647 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Async GRPO with LoRA across HF Jobs: a bucket, a proxy, and no NCCL

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LoRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14.
  • LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret.
  • There is also a systems consequence of LoRA training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LoRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14. The asynchronous trainer can now train an adapter instead of the full model, and it syncs only the LoRA adapter to vLLM. This post covers a real-world project built on top of it, where training and inference no longer share a machine.

LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

There is also a systems consequence of LoRA training. A rank-1 adapter for a 1.5B model is a few megabytes, while the full model is around 3 GB. Instead of sending the full policy to the inference workers after every enhancement, we can just send the adapter. vLLM can also keep several adapters loaded at once. Old rollouts finish with the policy they started with, while upcoming rollouts use the latest one.

TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer already separates training and generation. The trainer and vLLM can run on different machines and at their own speed. This is easy in a single-node or cluster setting where both processes share a filesystem or can form an NCCL group.

Recent findings suggest that what we want is to run the same setup with Hugging Face Jobs. Essentially, an HF Job is one container running on one VM. This means that one Job cannot spawn multiple nodes (at least for now) to hold a trainer and a fleet of vLLM servers (we are limited to 8xH200 at most per node). The AsyncGRPOTrainer is built for exactly that kind of scale, so the question became: how far can we get if we drop the requirement that the trainer and the inference servers share a node?

It has been revealed that well, with a full-weight sync, the answer would be "not far". Every update would have to move gigabytes between machines, which is what NCCL is for in a dense cluster, but Jobs can't communicate across nodes. There is no shared local disk and obviously no shared localhost. With LoRA, a sync is only a few megabytes. For the filesystem part, HF Jobs provide volumes backed by Storage Buckets! These buckets can then be mounted as a FUSE filesystem in every Job and are enough to work as a shared FS between nodes. No network path between the Jobs is needed at all.

The setup ended up being quite small:.

The upcoming adapter-only sync path in AsyncGRPOTrainer works like this. The trainer does not send tensors to vLLM. Every few optimizer steps, it saves the adapter under /.vllm_lora/trl-policy-v{N}, publishes the directory with an atomic rename, then sends its path to vLLM's /v1/load_lora_adapter endpoint. vLLM loads the files from disk, so the rollout worker can then request model="trl-policy-v{N}".

This is how runtime adapter loading already works in vLLM. The endpoint takes a path, not tensors, so the trainer and the server are expected to share a filesystem. On a Slurm cluster, that is the network filesystem. On Jobs, we get the same thing by mounting a Storage Bucket as a volume at the same path in every Job, as we mentioned earlier. Under the hood, it uses hf-mount, which exposes the bucket as a POSIX filesystem inside the container:.

Recent findings suggest that nothing in TRL or vLLM had to change for this. The trainer writes to /lora//.vllm_lora/ and the servers read from the same path. The path sent in the POST request is already valid inside every container.

Note that we also store the checkpoints and the final adapter in the bucket. The HF Jobs are ephemeral, but a preempted trainer can resume training, as the final adapter is always persisted to the bucket and is never lost when the Job stops.

In a recent development, each replica uses one GPU and the stock vllm/vllm-openai image. We only need to enable runtime LoRA loading and reserve enough adapter slots.

Recent findings suggest that the number of adapter slots follows from max_staleness. In AsyncGRPOTrainer, every weight sync bumps the policy version by one, and max_staleness is how many versions a rollout sample may lag behind the current policy before the trainer discards it. With max_staleness=4, a sample generated under trl-policy-v3 is still used for training while the trainer is at v7. A rollout that started under v3 must also be able to finish under v3. So at any moment, vLLM has to serve the current policy plus the four before it. That is why the trainer keeps max_staleness + 1 adapter versions registered and unloads anything older. Each sync loads the newly introduced version before it unloads the oldest one, which needs one more slot during the swap. That gives --max-loras 6. With only five, vLLM would silently evict a policy that still has rollouts in flight at every sync.

Recent findings suggest that we pin vLLM to v0.27.1. vLLM moves fast, and the flags above and the runtime LoRA endpoints are the ones that version exposes, so treat the version as part of the recipe.

In a recent development, there is another possible design where the trainer keeps only the latest adapter and always publishes it under the same name. We did not go that way, because vLLM keys its prefix cache by adapter name. With a single name, KV blocks computed under the previous weights would still match after the swap, so the prefill would not be redone and a rollout could get its prefix from one policy version and its decode from the next. The trainer would have no way to tell, and it would show up as ratio drifting away from 1. Versioned names make this impossible: a name always means one set of weights, and a cached prefix can never match a newer version.

Recent findings suggest that we chose sail/Sanity-Test-R1D-1.5B, the dataset from Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16 (Qi et al., 2025). The reproduction code is in sail-sg/Precision-RL.

Industry observers note that the authors generated 40 answers for each MATH problem with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. They kept problems with a success rate between 20% and 80%, yielding 1,460 questions. This dataset is really good for RL validation because the questions are neither already solved nor completely hopeless for that model, meaning the model can get a good early signal to train on and improve.

It has been revealed that this is awesome as a robust end-to-end test: if one vLLM replica silently serves the base model under an adapter name, we want to see that in the curve within a few dozen steps. Also, this dataset is small enough to cycle through in less than two hours.

We also take the hyperparameters from the paper's LoRA scripts in oat/scripts/lora: Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA rank 1 with alpha 2, a learning rate of 4e-5, 8 samples per prompt, 128 completions per step, a maximum of 3,000 generated tokens and a 4,096-token context.

The trainer uses the same vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1 image with TRL installed on top. We ran the PR branch at the time; the same code now ships in TRL v1.14. The training script is a normal AsyncGRPOTrainer script. The only Job-specific values are the output directory and the server URL.

During initialization, TRL calls /server_info. If it finds a lora_config, it uses adapter-only sync. Configurations vLLM cannot serve directly, such as DoRA, modules_to_save, or a rank above --max-lora-rank, fall back to merged-weight sync with a warning. The log should contain Adapter-only vLLM sync enabled.

According to recent reports, now onto the fun stuff. We need a proxy between the trainer and the vLLM Jobs for two reasons:.

In a recent development, exposed Job ports require an Authorization: Bearer header on every request. The proxy is where that header gets added, so TRL does not need to know about it.

It has been revealed that we want more than one GPU generating. On a single vLLM server, the usual way to get that is --data-parallel-size > 1, but TRL refuses adapter-only sync in that mode, for a good reason: a call to /v1/load_lora_adapter only reaches the DP rank that answers it, so the other ranks would keep serving the base model under the new policy name. On Jobs the question does not even arise, since each replica is its own machine. So the data parallelism has to live one level up, in something that fans the adapter load out to every replica.

We therefore run a small proxy at 127.0.0.1:8000 on the trainer Job and point TRL to it as if it were a single vLLM server. Besides adding the header, the proxy does two things functionally:.

A quick reminder of why this matters. Generating a completion has two phases with very different workload profiles:.

In a recent development, those keys and values are the KV cache. Because attention is causal, the KV of a token depends only on the tokens before it, not on what comes after. Two requests that share a prefix therefore share the KV of that prefix, and a replica that already has it in cache can skip that part of the prefill entirely. The whole game now is to find that replica, so a request can benefit from landing on the replica that has already seen its prefix.

In a recent development, vLLM stores its prefix KV cache in blocks of 16 tokens. Because of GRPO, the rollout worker sends G requests with the same prompt (in our case G=8). If they all reach the same replica, the first request computes the prefill and the next seven reuse it. With round-robin routing, half would go to a replica that doesn't have the prefix cached, and those four requests would redo the prefill work and waste valuable GPU compute.

The job of our router is to track which replica has seen which block hash. One crucial detail is that the hashes are chained, so the hash of block 3 represents blocks 1, 2 and 3, not just block 3. This mirrors causal attention: the KV of block 3 is only valid if blocks 1 and 2 are the same too. We also seed the chain with the adapter name because the KV cache also depends on the adapter that generated it: a prefix cached for policy v3 is useless for policy v4!

Recent findings suggest that the video walks through the entire decision process for choosing a replica. The steps below go through a real 135-token completion request example (from the Sanity dataset problems):.

1. Split the prompt into blocks. The router receives token ids and cuts them into 16-token blocks, just like vLLM. It only hashes complete blocks, so the last 7 tokens are ignored here.

2. Hash the prefix. Each block is hashed with the previous hash, starting from the adapter seed. h3 therefore identifies blocks 1, 2 and 3 in order. Two prompts with the same first k blocks get the same hashes up to hk. Once one block changes, every hash after it changes too. This is why we seed the hashes with the adapter name: the same prompt under trl-policy-v4 starts from another seed and cannot match entries from v3. This is what we want because the old KV blocks were computed with different weights.

3. Compare two prompts. Problem 1 has 103 tokens. Both prompts start with the same 23-token chat template. Their first block is identical, but block 2 already contains the problem text. The hashes differ from there.

Sources indicate that 4. Store the owners. For every hash, the router remembers which replicas served it and which hashes came after it (we cap the successor set at two because we only need to know whether a block has one continuation or several). After a few prompts, the template block h1 is owned by both replicas and already has several successors, h2 to h8 are owned by A only and each has a single successor, and h2' to h6' are owned by B only.

In practice, every prompt in a run starts with the same tokens. Here, it is the chat template and the system prompt, which amount to the first 23 tokens of all 1,460 problems. In an agent setting, it would be the tool descriptions, and in a multi-turn environment it would be the shared conversation history. These blocks are in every replica's cache within seconds, so matching on them tells us nothing about where a particular prompt lives.

A block is common if every replica has served it, or if it has more than one successor. Common blocks are ignored during routing because they do not identify a particular prompt. More on this below!

5. Pick a replica. The router counts how many leading blocks match on each replica and removes the common prefix. What is left is the number of blocks specific to this prompt. Then:.

Recent findings suggest that here is the rule applied to four requests. Start from a state where replicas A and B both have 3 requests in flight, and only the template block h1 is known on both replicas.

6. Reuse the prefill. Request 2 is the reason for doing all this. It reuses the prefill computed by Request 1: blocks 1 to 8 are already in A's KV cache, so A skips straight to decoding the completion. Had it gone to B, B would have prefilled all 135 tokens again while A's cache sat unused. Request 3 highlights why the common rule is needed. Without it, the shared chat template would make every new prompt look like a cache hit. Request 4 keeps the load bounded. Saving one prefill is not worth letting a replica fall far behind.

It has been revealed that the common prefix is the annoying part. Every request starts with the same system prompt and chat template. A simple longest-prefix match would give the first replica a match for almost every new prompt. We detect the shared prefix through fan-out instead: a block with several different successors is common, while a block that always leads to the same successor belongs to a particular prompt. Only the blocks after that common prefix count as affinity.

It has been revealed that the proxy also needs to broadcast the adapter loads to every replica. We treat the operation as all-or-nothing. Each replica has its own bucket mount, so they do not necessarily see a upcoming adapter at exactly the same time. A No adapter found for error usually means that one bucket mount has not caught up yet, and we retry only that replica. For any other error, we unload the adapter from the replicas that accepted it so that a policy name never exists on only part of the replicas.

It has been revealed that we also broadcast /pause, /resume and /v1/unload_lora_adapter in the same way. /health returns 200 only if every replica is healthy. /server_info and /v1/models only need one answer. From TRL's point of view, the proxy is a single data_parallel_size=1 server, so it selects adapter-only sync.

Sources indicate that we initially wondered whether a Python asyncio proxy would become a bottleneck. It does not (at least at this scale). There are at most 128 non-streaming JSON requests in flight, and routing only computes a few hashes. One thread handles this easily. A more refined router that needs to handle more traffic would probably need to be written in a faster language (We see you 🦀).

Industry observers note that the numbers below come from the trainer's logged metrics on trackio. The run uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA r=1 on all-linear, 128 completions per step and 8 rollouts per prompt. It runs for 500 steps and saves a checkpoint every 50 steps. The trainer uses an h200x2 Job and each of the two vLLM replicas uses one h200 Job. Running all three costs ~$20 per hour.

Sources indicate that all 252 adapter loads succeeded 🎉: 126 syncs times 2 replicas. Six succeeded on the second attempt and 246 on the third.

At the end of the run, after 64,728 rollouts, the proxy's counters read:.

With 8 rollouts per prompt, at least one of the eight requests must be cold. The theoretical minimum is therefore 12.5 %. The router gets 14.2 % unmatched requests, 84.5 % affinity hits, and 1.3 % spills. There is not much left to gain here unless we start looking at each replica's load using deeper inference-side metrics based on real measured load.

Recent findings suggest that the first configuration has a pretty obvious problem: the trainer is the bottleneck, not generation. Over the 500 steps, we have:.

According to recent reports, the rollout queue stays full, and the worker is mostly blocked by backpressure. The second replica is basically useless in this configuration. We'll see later in the post how we went through runs that moved the bottleneck between training and generation to make the run 3.9× faster.

Figure 1. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: reward with its 20-step rolling mean and 50-step block means, and ratio on a 0.99 to 1.01 axis. Reward climbs from 0.15 to 0.44 over 500 steps; ratio stays between 0.9993 and 1.0004 throughout.

Sources indicate that 500 steps took 3 h 27 min. Mean reward goes from 0.145 over the first 20 steps to 0.438 over the last 20. More importantly for this test, ratio stays at 1.000 for every step! The policy served by vLLM always matches the one used by the trainer to score the rollout. This held across all 126 syncs. Mean staleness was 1.5 policy versions, against a maximum of 4. The trackio dashboard has the full curves.

We have our undeniable proof that LoRA AsyncGRPO works! Let's now see how we can improve our training runs by looking at the recent detailed AsyncGRPO metrics.

Async RL is a pipeline between training and generation. Making one side faster does nothing if the other side cannot keep up. Fortunately, in AsyncGRPOTrainer we've added enough timings and metrics to see this directly.

All the useful metrics are documented in the Logged metrics section. perf/rollout_wait_s tells us how long the trainer waits for samples. rollout/backpressure_s tells us how long generation waits for space in the rollout queue. They are diametrically opposed to each other and should not both be high. Together with the queue size, they tell us which side is slow.

In a recent development, we ran five experiments. Each one starts from a problem visible in the previous run's dashboard. Unless mentioned otherwise, the model, recipe and three-Job layout stay the same. The names below are the trackio run names.

We keep these four groups of metrics visible:.

The diagnosis is simple: a full queue with zero rollout wait and high backpressure means the trainer is too slow. An empty queue with rising rollout wait and no backpressure means generation is too slow. Comparing perf/mfu_wall_clock with perf/mfu_fwd_bwd also reveals how much time the trainer GPUs spend waiting instead of training.

Figure 2. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, rollout/backpressure_s. Step time and forward+backward overlap almost completely; the queue sits pinned near 476 of 512 and backpressure never drops below 11 s per rollout group: trainer-bound.

perf/step_s is 22.9 s and perf/fwd_bwd_s is 21.9 s. Forward and backward take 96 % of the step time. The queue stays full and the trainer waits only 0.02 s for rollouts, and the rollout worker spends 15 seconds per group blocked by backpressure. The two vLLM replicas generate faster than the trainer consumes. The reported 4.6k tokens/s is not their actual limit; they simply have nowhere to put more output.

According to recent reports, the batch metrics explain the terrible 3.9 % MFU. batch/microbatches_per_step is 64 and batch/samples_per_row is 1.0. Each rank processes one sequence of around 1.2k tokens, 64 times per step. This comes from the reference recipe's per_device_train_batch_size=1. For a 1.5B model on an H200, this is completely latency-bound.

Recent findings suggest that the fix is not to change the batch size. We keep 128 completions per optimizer step and only change how they are laid out on the GPU: instead of one sequence per microbatch, we pack many sequences densely into each row. The trainer supports this through token-budget batching. With token_budget > 0, it packs several samples into one padding-free row per rank. An optimizer step processes gradient_accumulation_steps rows. We set token_budget=16384 and gradient_accumulation_steps=6.

Figure 3. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp2-tb16k overlaid over their first 154 steps. Panels: batch/samples_per_row, batch/microbatches_per_step, perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd, rollout/generated_tok_s. Packing takes samples per row from 1 to 13, microbatches from 64 to 6, step time from 23 s to 5.9 s, and generation from 4.2k to 27.5k tok/s with no change on the vLLM side.

Sources indicate that batch/samples_per_row goes from 1.0 to ~12.7 and the number of microbatches drops from 64 to 6. The rows are 95 % full! Forward and backward fall from 21.9 s to 5.6 s, while MFU rises from 3.9 % to 19 %. We now train on around 150 samples per step because the rows pack better than the mean-length estimate predicted.

Recent findings suggest that generation also jumps from 4.6k to 25k tokens/s, even though we changed nothing on the vLLM side. The queue is no longer constantly full, so the replicas can finally run. This is why we do not like optimizing pipeline stages in isolation. We need to be careful to evaluate the whole system, as a slow stage can hide the real performance of everything before it.

Recent findings suggest that perf/fwd_s is 1.34 s while perf/fwd_bwd_s is 5.6 s. A normal backward costs roughly twice the forward, and with frozen base weights it should be closer to once. A ratio of 3.2 is suspicious.

In a recent development, the reason is that AsyncGRPOConfig defaults to gradient_checkpointing=True. Every microbatch recomputes its forward during the backward. This also explains why a 16k-token row only uses 25 GB on a 141 GB H200! It's a memory optimization for this trainer, but we don't need it in this specific case: the model is small enough to fit into VRAM with the activations kept for the backward.

Figure 4. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k and r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/fwd_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/weight_sync_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, perf/rollout_wait_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd. Forward+backward drops by one forward; the queue falls from ~420 to ~60, and rollout wait rises from 0.02 s to 0.5 s: the bottleneck shifts to generation.

Industry observers note that with gradient_checkpointing=False, forward and backward drop to 4.6 s, almost exactly one forward less, and MFU reaches 23 %. The queue now falls to 71 and rollout wait rises from 0.04 s to 0.6 s. The trainer consumes samples faster than two replicas generate them. We successfully moved the bottleneck to generation.

According to recent reports, this exposes two more costs. A 7.6-second weight sync every four steps now takes 25 % of wall-clock time. It was only 8 % when each step took 23 seconds. Also, backward is still 2.5 times slower than forward. With frozen base weights, there are around 2 seconds per step that do not look like normal model math.

It has been revealed that since generation was now too slow, we added a third replica. We also reduced the adapter retry interval from 2 s to 0.5 s in the proxy and disabled fsdp_reshard_after_forward to check whether FSDP2 re-gathers caused the extra 2 seconds in backward.

Figure 5. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt and r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/weight_sync_s, rollout/generated_tok_s, rollout/inflight, perf/fwd_bwd_s. Sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s; generation and forward+backward do not move; rollout/inflight reads 128 in both runs, which is the cap the third replica ran into.

Sources indicate that weight sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s, so the shorter retry helps. Forward and backward stay at 4.6 s, which rules out resharding. Generation moves from 25k to only 26k tokens/s. The third replica does basically nothing.

In a recent development, the reason was sitting in rollout/inflight: 128 in every run. The proxy highlights those requests split as 44 + 43 + 41 across the three replicas. max_inflight_tasks limits concurrency for the whole rollout worker, not per replica. A 1.5B model on an H200 processes 43 and 130 concurrent sequences at almost the same cost per token. Splitting 128 requests over three GPUs gives nearly the same throughput as splitting them over two.

So vLLM was not the limit. Our own client-side constant was. We had set it conservatively because we did not know how hundreds of long HTTPS requests would behave through the public Jobs proxy. At this point, 130,000 rollout completions had crossed it without a single transport error.

max_inflight_tasks=384 and queue_maxsize=768, nothing else.

Industry observers note that figure 6. All five trackio runs (r1-dp2, r1-dp2-tb16k, r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-inflight384) overlaid, x-axis in steps. Panels: perf/step_s, reward, sample/rollout_queue_size, sample/staleness_mean. Step time falls from 22.9 s to 4.8 s across the series while the reward curves stay on top of each other; the last run's queue refills to ~690 of 768 and its staleness settles at 2. Runs 2 to 4 were stopped early once the dashboard had answered the question.

With 384 requests in flight, each replica gets 128. The queue rapidly fills to around 690 out of 768 and stays there. Backpressure returns to 5 seconds and rollout wait falls to 0.03 seconds. Training is the bottleneck again! Forward and backward take 4.6 seconds, weight sync adds an amortized 1.5 seconds, and median step time is 4.8 seconds.

Sources indicate that mean staleness rises from 1.5 to 2.0 versions because samples wait longer in the larger queue. This is still below max_staleness=4, and ratio remains very close to 1.000.

Figure 7. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp3-inflight384, reward against wall-clock minutes since the first optimizer step. Same recipe, same 500 steps, same final reward; run 5 gets there in 52 minutes instead of 3 h 26 min.

Sources indicate that the final run is 3.9× faster and trains on 31 % more samples, with basically the same reward curve. Packing, disabling checkpointing and raising the in-flight limit made the difference. In each case, the dashboard made this clear within the first ten minutes.

LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with sportzfy rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

Really interesting take on how LoRA changes the systems side of RL training, not just the training itself. The idea of separating training and inference across different machines while only moving a small adapter instead of the full model makes a lot of practical sense, especially when working with HF Jobs. The “bucket, proxy, and no NCCL” approach feels like a good example of simplifying distributed infrastructure by moving the communication boundary to something much smaller and easier to manage.

I also like the connection to the LoRA Without Regret work, particularly the point that policy-gradient updates may not require huge adapter capacity to capture the useful signal. Sending only a few MB instead of several GB after updates can make a massive difference in both bandwidth and iteration speed. Would be really interested to see more details on how the bucket/proxy setup behaves at scale and whether there are any noticeable trade-offs once the number of inference workers or concurrent rollouts increases.

#92425. iTerm2 Arbitrary Command Execution via Kitty Image Protocol APC Response Injection

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (945 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

iTerm2 Arbitrary Command Execution via Kitty Image Protocol APC Response Injection

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (945 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • iTerm2’s Kitty image protocol implementation has an arbitrary command execution vulnerability in the file transmit error response path.
  • Three independent issues combine into a single exploit chain: (1) the APC handler lacks the trust check present in OSC handlers, (2) the Kitty file transmit error path preserves literal newlines from NSError.localizedDescription, and (3) the response is unconditionally written to PTY stdin.
  • When the VT100 parser receives an APC sequence, it calls executeAPC:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iTerm2’s Kitty image protocol implementation has an arbitrary command execution vulnerability in the file transmit error response path. An APC escape sequence embedded in any file is consumed by the VT100 parser and does not appear in the cat output itself, but the Kitty file transmit error response preserves literal newlines from a crafted file path and writes them to PTY stdin — the shell interprets these newlines as command separators, resulting in arbitrary command execution. This is a logic bug — no memory corruption or race condition required — and is 100% reproducible. It works on a default iTerm2 installation with no configuration changes, and triggers on all shells including bash, zsh, and fish.

Three independent issues combine into a single exploit chain: (1) the APC handler lacks the trust check present in OSC handlers, (2) the Kitty file transmit error path preserves literal newlines from NSError.localizedDescription, and (3) the response is unconditionally written to PTY stdin.

When the VT100 parser receives an APC sequence, it calls executeAPC:. At [A], it checks for tmux mode — if active, it returns early. At [B], it checks only whether the string starts with “G”, and at [C] creates a Kitty image command and passes it to the delegate. Compared to OSC sequence handling, the terminalIsTrusted check is completely absent. Any APC that reaches the VT100 parser is unconditionally executed regardless of source.

Sources indicate that no trust check exists in the delegate chain either. At [A], the command is passed directly to kittyImageController.

When the Kitty image controller receives a t=f (file transmit) command, it decodes the base64 payload and uses it as a file path. At [A], URL.resourceValues() checks whether the file exists — if it doesn’t, an exception is thrown. At [B], the filenameIsSafe() blocklist check exists, but this code is only reachable after resourceValues() succeeds, so it never executes for non-existent files. At [C], the catch block embeds error.localizedDescription directly into the error message. macOS’s NSError.localizedDescription preserves literal newlines (0x0A) in filenames without escaping them.

The response containing the error message is written to PTY stdin. At [A], the default verbosity .normal always sends the response — it is sent regardless of whether it is an error. At [B], the response is wrapped in APC format (ESC_G...ESC\) and passed to the delegate.

At the end of the delegate chain, [A] the response data is written to the PTY via screenSendReportData:. This function sends data through the same path as keyboard input, so the shell interprets this data as if the user typed it.

The developer confirmed and fixed the vulnerability across two commits. Adding a terminalIsTrusted check to the APC handler would not have protected default installations — terminalIsTrusted is simply the inverse of the advanced setting “Disable potentially insecure escape sequences,” which is off by default (the terminal is trusted by default). The response sanitization is what closes the hole for everyone.

Sources indicate that the first fix adds sanitizedResponseMessage(_:) to KittyImageController.swift. It replaces every C0 control character (0x00–0x1F, including ESC, CR, LF) and DEL (0x7F) with a space before the response is framed and sent. The error payload in respondToTransmit() and respondToDisplay() is passed through this sanitizer. a53b1bc.

In a recent development, the follow-up commit extracts a shared sanitizer stringByReplacingControlCharactersWithSpace on NSString, extending coverage to C1 characters (0x80–0x9F) while preserving Unicode format characters (Cf) such as ZWJ and bidi marks. It replaces the per-file sanitizer and is applied to three report paths: Kitty image, Kitty drag-and-drop (OSC 72), and title reporting. 2a63835.

The Kitty drag-and-drop sanitizer was changed from stripping only CR/LF to stripping all control characters, and the title report sanitizer was hardened the same way.

The attack vector is embedding APC escape sequence bytes into a malicious file. When the entire file content is output to the terminal (e.g., via cat), the raw bytes are delivered to the terminal and processed by the VT100 parser. This works on all shells — bash, zsh, fish, etc. — the shell type is irrelevant.

It has been revealed that the APC sequence (starting with ESC _, ending with ESC \) is consumed by iTerm2’s VT100 parser and is invisible in the cat output — the file appears to be a normal document. However, when the exploit triggers, the error response injected into PTY stdin produces visible garbled shell errors on the terminal. The injected command executes between these garbled lines, so the command execution itself is visible to the user. Concealment of this output was not explored in this research.

The core of the attack relies on two facts: macOS NSError.localizedDescription preserves literal newlines in filenames, and the error message uses curly quotes instead of ASCII double-quotes.

Why ASCII double-quotes are not used: If ASCII " is included in the file path, it appears as-is in the error message. When delivered to the shell via PTY, bash enters double-quote mode upon encountering ", and newlines no longer act as command separators. macOS’s NSError.localizedDescription uses Unicode curly quotes (“, ”), which are not special characters in bash and do not trigger quote mode.

The file path set by the attacker (before base64 encoding):.

Recent findings suggest that APC bytes can be embedded in any file type — .md, .txt, .log, .csv, configuration files, source code, etc. The only requirement is that the file content is output to the terminal via cat. The following example uses a README.md, but any file that a user might cat is a valid vector. The APC itself is invisible in cat output (consumed by the VT100 parser), but the error response injected into PTY stdin appears as garbled shell errors alongside the executed command.

#92423. Beyond Linux: A Journey Through the Open Source Ecosystem

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4780 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dragas ↗ Open Full Page

Beyond Linux: A Journey Through the Open Source Ecosystem

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dragas

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that what follows is the text of the talk I gave at Linux Day 2026 in Modena, lightly adapted for the blog.
  • Linux is one of the best-known players in the open source world, but it's not the only possible path.
  • I'm a sysadmin and consultant, and I run my own small company specialised in open source services and solutions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that what follows is the text of the talk I gave at Linux Day 2026 in Modena, lightly adapted for the blog. The talk was in Italian, in front of a Linux audience - which explains a few of the jokes.

Linux is one of the best-known players in the open source world, but it's not the only possible path. A journey through the BSDs, illumos and other alternative operating systems, to reflect on Open Source as an idea, a philosophy and a practice of sharing knowledge.

My name is Stefano Marinelli. I'm a sysadmin and consultant, and I run my own small company specialised in open source services and solutions. I like to call myself the "Barista" of the BSD Cafe and the illumos Cafe, online communities of people passionate about technology, open source and sharing. Today I'm not here just to talk about operating systems, but about freedom, sharing and knowledge. From free software to open source.

My first contact with the Free Software world was in 1996, when I wasn't even 17 yet. I saw a box set advertised in a magazine: "a whole operating system, for free", at a very low price. Something like 30,000 lire. Shortly before, I'd paid roughly ten times as much for the Windows 95 upgrade edition. Dismissive and without a shred of trust, I decided to order it and give it a go. I mean: who would ever write something like that... and release the source code? But six CDs for 30,000 lire... let's try. Worst case, it'll be an experience.

It was love at first shell. That terminal opened up a whole universe, and to what I already knew (commercial licences, freeware, shareware) I added the concept of Free Software. But I didn't have enough hardware to run two operating systems, so I reinstalled Windows and put it all off. Still, I started thinking. Reflecting. Studying. In 1997 I got a new PC and started using Linux - or, as I was careful to say, GNU/Linux - for everything. Except games. For those, a small Windows partition survived, though not for long.

According to recent reports, in 1998 I enrolled in Computer Science at the University of Bologna. Even back then, it was a faculty strongly oriented towards free software. Linux in the labs. I was one of the few who, in the first year, already knew what Free Software was (not free as in price, but...freedom!) and how to use the Linux workstations. That gave me a big advantage, especially from the second year onwards. Renzo Davoli was already pushing hard in that direction. I decided that would be my path. And so it was, and I started pushing too. Windows wasn't the "enemy" to me. The imposition was. Personally, I respect rules, but not impositions. Some people followed me, others watched from a distance. I didn't care. I was widening my horizons.

In the early 2000s I also discovered the BSDs. And I convinced my parents that I needed a laser printer for "university material". In reality, I wanted to print the excellent BSD documentation. Maybe not university material, but the printed FreeBSD Handbook probably served me better than half of the theory exams I took back then. Thanks, mom and dad!

But let's get back to the beginning.

Free Software was born out of a change. In those days, code circulated freely among people. Depending on their needs, they exchanged source code, modified it and shared it again. But at some point this began to change. There's an anecdote that, while not exhaustive, gives the idea: the printer Richard Stallman was using kept jamming, and nobody got notified. He wanted to modify the software so that he'd get a notification, as he'd done with the previous printer. Back then it was common practice, but this time he was refused. "I can't share the source code. It's under NDA." In other words, he had lost control over what he was using. He even wanted to improve the program, and instead he got a refusal.

Industry observers note that the rest is history. At least until a few years ago.

Because thirty years ago we fought for Free Software to be taken seriously. When I started working, I was almost laughed at. "That's toy stuff you use at university. The real world uses something else." "Why don't you just use Windows? Everything's easier." And yet, the toys often worked better than the expensive proprietary solutions. Or at least just as well, at a fraction of the cost. "Let's try. Don't pay me until you're satisfied." They smiled, incredulous. Then they paid, happily. We could prove there was an alternative. Free, with no artificial locks. Something that anyone - even the broke but eager student - could study and set up. Technology, that kind of "enterprise" technology, was truly within everyone's reach. There was no need to buy expensive products, or recurring certifications just to have the "right" to work on them. You study, you apply yourself, nobody can stop you. I attended Linux Days. I spoke at Linux Days. For example, here I am, in Linux Day 2004.

We won that battle. We won that war. Linux - chaotic Linux, built by countless external contributors, made of different and varied distributions - has reached everywhere. Open Source is everywhere. But something happened - something beautiful, but terrible: precisely because it reached everywhere, something changed in the spirit. "Too big to fail". And so the big players arrived. Today, Linux development is driven by corporate money: companies like Microsoft (the same Microsoft that once considered Linux its sworn enemy - or Red Hat itself) and other big tech players. In itself, this has been a good thing. In practice, though, it means that they steer its development, even if indirectly. Year after year, it has started to take the shape of a different kind of product. Is the user still at the centre, or is it more code to make Azure run better? Sure, it's Open Source, it's free. But it's increasingly close to the needs of the big companies funding its development and, at times, further from the ordinary user. That's not necessarily bad: many of these investments have given us extraordinary technologies.

But I wonder whether, in the process, we're losing something. Not so much in the code as in the mindset. If not in the kernel, then in the community around it.

Recent findings suggest that back then, precisely because we were frustrated by "It only works on Windows", we were careful to write portable software. I'll say one word, without going into too much detail: POSIX. Once a mantra: POSIX compliant. A set of standards defining common interfaces between operating systems, so you can write programs that, with few or even no changes, run on different Unix and Unix-like systems. Today, in the communities around Linux, you hear more and more often that POSIX is "outdated". When I send a patch to make a specific tool work on FreeBSD, for example, I often read comments like: "Why don't you just use Linux?". And that dÃ©jÃ  vu sends a shiver down my spine: is the community I loved so much turning into a copy, albeit a better one, of its worst enemy?

But careful: I'm not here to speak ill of Linux. That would be absurd. I mean: coming to Linux Day to trash Linux? It's an extraordinary operating system, and I owe it a great deal.

I'm here to remind you that Linux isn't the only way to understand free software. And that a project being less well known doesn't make it less interesting, less valid or less worthy of attention. Because if freedom of choice is truly a value, we must be ready to defend it even when someone chooses something different from what we choose.

So let's see what lies beyond Linux. Because monoculture is a problem, in Open Source too.

Industry observers note that because free software is...free. And we must be free too. Free to choose, to consider alternatives. To contribute, if we want to. To understand which solution best fits our problem. We don't have to pick a single solution "because everyone does". We don't have to turn one monopoly into another. Linux is great. It helps put bread on my table, so I'm a fan. But there are alternatives, other solutions, that can have their advantages. And that's why I want to talk to you about the BSDs and illumos.

Recent findings suggest that BSD stands for Berkeley Software Distribution. And the first curious thing is that its story begins before Linux even existed. We're in the late Seventies. At the University of California, Berkeley, some researchers are working on UNIX, the operating system developed at AT&T's Bell Labs. They don't just use it. They modify it, improve it, write new programs and share that work with other universities.

Recent findings suggest that remind you of something? We've just been talking about Stallman and the culture of sharing.

Sources indicate that BSD was born in exactly that world. So it was born on solid, stable, reliable foundations. Studied by experts, not as a game. BSD was an operating system directly related to Unix. It was a complete and stable system, but it wasn't yet available for "home" systems, the i386 family. Born well before Linux. A curiosity: Linus Torvalds himself, in a 1993 interview, noted: "If 386BSD had been available when I started on Linux, Linux would probably never had happened.". Yes, you heard that right. Linus Torvalds said it. And we're at a Linux Day!

Sources indicate that then something happened: BSD arrived on the i386, and Unix System Laboratories, controlled by AT&T, started a rather insidious legal dispute: there's our code in BSD and you have no right to use, modify or share it. The University of California was dragged into it too. This was a real blocker for many. Companies were afraid to adopt an operating system with a lawsuit like that in progress. The matter dragged on until 1994, when a settlement was reached and 4.4BSD-Lite was released, with a freely redistributable and legally cleared base.

Meanwhile, Linux was growing, attracting developers, winning users. It didn't have that particular legal uncertainty. I'm not saying Linux succeeded only because of this. That would be unfair to Torvalds and to the thousands of people who contributed to its development.

Industry observers note that but it's interesting to think that the history of computing as we know it could have taken a different path. And it's also interesting that, despite these difficulties, BSD didn't disappear. Quite the opposite.

From that story came some of the operating systems I want to talk about today. Systems that took different paths and that are still developed, used and improved. Different operating systems - careful, not distributions of the same operating system! - each unique in its own way. Let's start with FreeBSD.

FreeBSD is probably the most general-purpose BSD. It's a complete operating system, designed to offer stability, performance and a certain consistency in administration. And here's a first difference from Linux I'd like to highlight. In the BSDs, the kernel and the userland, the base tools of the operating system, are developed and maintained within the same project. That doesn't mean Linux works worse. It means the development model is different.

And there's a philosophy I really appreciate: evolution, not revolution. It doesn't mean standing still. It means trying to improve without necessarily turning upside down what already works.

According to recent reports, let's talk about some technologies. ZFS, for example. An advanced filesystem, with snapshots, data integrity, replication and many other features. FreeBSD integrates it directly into the system and also lets you use Boot Environments: I can upgrade the system and, if something goes wrong, go back to the previous environment.

Then we have jails. FreeBSD has had a technology for isolating processes, resources and application environments since 2000. Long before Docker arrived. Jails aren't Docker, and I'm not saying they're the same thing. But they let you isolate applications and services simply, with low overhead, using the operating system's own features directly. A bit like LXC on Linux.

It has been revealed that for virtualisation we have bhyve, which lets you run virtual machines, including other operating systems. And bhyve is lighter and, often, faster than KVM on Linux. [LINK: my bhyve articles].

Sources indicate that but FreeBSD isn't just a system for enthusiasts. Netflix uses it to deliver video content. PlayStation consoles have a FreeBSD-derived base. macOS and iOS also include code from the BSD world. OPNsense and pfSense, two well-known firewall solutions, are based on FreeBSD. In short, we're not talking about a university toy. Remind you of something?

It has been revealed that personally, I've been using FreeBSD for many years, in production too. And it has often let me solve problems simply, while staying in control of what's happening. I've seen cases where, on the same hardware and with the same workload, FreeBSD handled I/O pressure better, with even very significant reductions in execution time. If you're curious, there are several articles about it here on IT Notes. That doesn't mean FreeBSD is always faster than Linux. That would be nonsense. It means there are situations where it can be the better choice.

Sources indicate that and for me, this is the point: I solve problems. I don't have to defend an operating system. I have to pick the right tool.

In a recent development, then there's OpenBSD. OpenBSD was born in 1995 as a fork of NetBSD and is probably one of the most interesting systems when we talk about security and code correctness.

According to recent reports, its philosophy is fairly simple: less complexity, fewer chances for mistakes. The code is continuously reviewed, cleaned up, simplified. Features aren't added just because they might be interesting. Every choice has to make sense within the project. Because the more complex code becomes, the harder it is to maintain, audit and verify.

OpenBSD has also developed some very interesting security mechanisms, like pledge() and unveil(), which let you restrict the operations a program can perform and the parts of the filesystem it can access.

According to recent reports, and then there's OpenSSH. Yes, the very OpenSSH you probably use every day to manage your servers. It was born, and is developed, within the OpenBSD project.

But there's another feature I love: the documentation. In the OpenBSD world, insufficient or wrong documentation is considered a bug. The man pages are often enough to understand how to use and configure the system, without hunting for guides of dubious quality scattered across the Internet. And believe me, when you manage dozens or hundreds of systems, knowing where to find correct and consistent information is a huge advantage.

OpenBSD doesn't try to please everyone. The developers follow their own priorities, even when that means giving up something other systems offer. Can it be frustrating? Certainly. But it also offers a great advantage: consistency, predictability and a clear design direction.

For firewalls, routers and systems where security is particularly crucial, it's an alternative always worth considering.

According to recent reports, netBSD, on the other hand, has a wonderful motto. "Of course it runs NetBSD!" And that already says a lot about its philosophy.

Industry observers note that netBSD puts a huge emphasis on portability, correctness of implementation and the ability to run on very different hardware architectures. Not just modern x86 or ARM computers. We're also talking about machines decades old, architectures many consider long forgotten. And careful: it's not just a matter of computing nostalgia.

Keeping an operating system working on such different platforms forces you to write code with great attention to portability, avoiding needless dependencies on a specific architecture.

Remember when, a moment ago, I was talking about POSIX and portability as a value? Well, NetBSD is one of the best examples of that philosophy. Because a system that can run on very different hardware must necessarily care about how correct, clean and portable its code is. And that has positive consequences on the more common platforms too.

It has been revealed that there's another aspect I appreciate: continuity. We don't always need the latest novelty, the latest feature, the latest framework. Some devices and applications simply need to keep working, maybe for many years. Think of embedded systems, small computers, hardware that isn't replaced every two years. In these contexts, knowing there's a project that considers portability and support for different architectures a fundamental part of its identity is reassuring.

In a recent development, it's a different philosophy from FreeBSD's and from OpenBSD's. And that's absolutely fine.

According to recent reports, netBSD has also taken a clear stance on AI-generated code: it can't be committed without prior written approval, because it's considered potentially "tainted" - both in form and in licence. And in today's extremely polarised world, that's a sigh of relief for anyone who wants to use and develop an operating system without the pressure of always having to do more, add more features and more code.

There's also DragonFlyBSD, born in 2003 as a fork of FreeBSD, which followed other design choices, especially regarding the kernel and system management. We don't have time to go into everything, but I want to stress one thing. These systems have common origins and share part of their history, but they don't necessarily have the same goals.

Industry observers note that freeBSD is a general-purpose system, also oriented towards performance and production environments. It's stable and secure. On the desktop it might not support all the hardware Linux does, although they're working on it. But on servers it could be one of the best alternatives to Linux.

OpenBSD favours security, simplicity and code correctness. NetBSD focuses heavily on portability and on supporting different hardware. DragonFlyBSD has experimented with other architectural solutions. And yet, they all belong to the big BSD family.

Recent findings suggest that there's no need for one to win over the others. It's not a battle. There's nothing to sell here. It's freedom. It's diversity. And that diversity is a strength.

If there's one thing I've learnt over all these years, it's exactly this: an operating system shouldn't be a religion. In my daily life, I solve problems. And to solve them, I need to be able to evaluate the alternatives.

Sources indicate that because stability, for example, isn't just a system's ability not to crash. It's also being able to update it without surprises, to understand how it works, to know what happens when something goes wrong. Observability is fundamental, and being able to have it without weaving together fifty Docker containers can sometimes make the difference between ten minutes of work and two hours.

According to recent reports, we don't always need to reinvent everything. What's newly introduced isn't always better. And the solution chosen by the majority isn't always the best fit for our problem. Often, it's exactly the opposite.

But our journey doesn't end with the BSDs.

There's another family of operating systems that descends from a different UNIX history. A history that runs through Sun Microsystems, Solaris and OpenSolaris. And that leads us to illumos.

Sources indicate that now someone might ask: weren't you talking about the BSDs? Yes, but the talk is called Beyond Linux, not Only BSD!

illumos isn't a BSD. It descends from another branch of the substantial UNIX family. The Solaris one, developed by Sun Microsystems. Sun. Anyone remember it? SPARC workstations, servers, Solaris, Java. In the Nineties and the 2000s it was one of the biggest names in professional computing.

According to recent reports, and Solaris was a very interesting operating system. Designed for serious machines, serious workloads, situations where a problem could cost a lot. In Bologna, when I was a student, there were some Solaris machines in the UnderLab. I looked at them sideways. To me they were "non-Linux". So I didn't like them.

Sources indicate that in 2005 Sun did something significant: it started publishing the Solaris source code through the OpenSolaris project. Imagine: a commercial UNIX system, with years of development behind it, advanced technologies and long experience in enterprise environments, opening up to the community. It wasn't the first free software to be used in companies, of course. But it was another way of doing things. Another model.

Recent findings suggest that and then, in 2010, Oracle acquired Sun. And here things changed. Oracle decided to stop the open development of OpenSolaris and stopped publishing new code updates.

Recent findings suggest that because the code that had already been released under an open source licence remained available. Oracle could decide not to publish its developments any more, but it couldn't take back the freedoms already granted on that code. And that's how illumos was born. A group of developers decided to carry on the work, starting from the open OpenSolaris base.

It has been revealed that think about it for a moment. A company acquires another company, changes strategy and stops the public development of an operating system. But that system doesn't die. Because the code exists, the skills exist, and there are people willing to keep working on it.

Remind you of something? We began this talk with Stallman and a printer whose code couldn't be shared. Thirty years later, the very possibility of sharing and modifying code allows a whole family of operating systems to keep existing.

This, for me, is one of the most beautiful aspects of free software.

According to recent reports, but let's get back to the technology. Because illumos isn't just a nice story.

From Solaris, illumos inherited some extremely interesting technologies. You already know one: ZFS. ZFS was born at Sun. It's a filesystem, but also a volume manager. It lets you manage storage, snapshots, data replication, integrity checks and much more.

I use ZFS practically everywhere I can. On FreeBSD, on illumos, on NetBSD and on Linux too. And that's already an example of how a good technology can cross different operating systems.

According to recent reports, then we have DTrace. DTrace lets you observe what's happening inside a system, even while it's running. We can analyse kernel calls, processes, performance, behaviours that would otherwise be hard to understand. For a sysadmin, it's an extraordinary tool. Because when a client tells you "the server is slow", the problem isn't knowing it's slow. They already know that. The problem is understanding why.

Then there are Zones. An isolation system that lets you run separate environments sharing the same kernel. Remember FreeBSD's jails? Well, zones were inspired by FreeBSD's jails. The concept is similar, although the implementations and some features differ.

And then Crossbow, for network virtualisation. SMF, for managing services and their dependencies. In short, we're talking about a system with vital technologies, born to tackle concrete problems. Not an experiment cobbled together in someone's spare time. And careful, I'm not saying these technologies are necessarily better than those available on Linux or the BSDs. I'm saying they're different, they have their own history and, in certain contexts, they can be particularly useful.

Like Linux, illumos is the base of several distributions, each with different features and goals.

Industry observers note that smartOS, for example, is focused on virtualisation. It has an interesting peculiarity: the operating system is loaded into RAM, from USB or from the network (or even from the local disk, but then it runs read-only), leaving the disks to the virtual machines and the data, managed with ZFS. It supports native Zones, LX zones to run Linux applications, and virtual machines via KVM and bhyve. Yes, the very bhyve we've already met talking about FreeBSD! Personally, I'm using and experimenting with it a lot. It's not all roses, but I really like some of its solutions. And bhyve on illumos even has a few gems that haven't been brought back to FreeBSD. Open Source and collaboration between projects, at their best!

OmniOS takes a more traditional road. It's an operating system designed mainly for servers, with particular attention to stability, updates and long-term continuity. It offers stable releases and long-term support versions. You install it, configure your services and use it. Without necessarily having to reinvent everything at every revision.

It has been revealed that openIndiana is perhaps the closest to the classic idea of a general-purpose UNIX distribution. It can be used on servers, but also as a desktop system, with a full graphical environment. For anyone who'd like to try a Solaris-derived system on their own computer, it could be an interesting starting point.

And then there's Tribblix, a rather special project. Created by Peter Tribble, it combines an almost nostalgic, traditional UNIX feel with modern components. It has its own package management system and a modular approach through overlays, which let you install groups of software. A small, independent system with a very precise personality.

Four distributions sharing a technological base, but interpreting it in different ways. Remind you of something? Linux... And that's exactly the point. There's no single way to build an operating system. There's no single development philosophy.

Recent findings suggest that and none of them needs to prevail over the others. What matters is that they keep existing, evolving and offering alternatives. Because, in the end, freedom of choice only has value if we really have something to choose from.

Industry observers note that because there's a whole UNIX tradition that isn't Linux and isn't BSD. Because some technologies now considered fundamental in modern computing were born right there. And, still today, they're stable and reliable. They're refined and polished without being "rewritten" or replaced every five years because there's a fresh fashion. Because we can use systems that followed different paths, with different architectures and design choices.

Recent findings suggest that but above all, because illumos is also a practical demonstration of the value of free software. Sun opened the code. Oracle decided to stop that open development. The community was able to carry on.

According to recent reports, it wasn't easy, and it doesn't mean every open source project can automatically survive the disappearance of whoever was funding it. You need developers, resources, skills. You need someone willing to take care of it. Available code is a necessary condition, but on its own it isn't enough.

Industry observers note that and this brings us to a point that, for me, is fundamental. Free software isn't just code. It's also the people who choose to develop it, maintain it, document it and share it.

That's why, alongside the BSD Cafe, I also wanted to create the illumos Cafe. To offer a space to meet, discuss and share experiences about technologies that maybe don't make the front pages of tech sites every day.

Recent findings suggest that because we don't all have to use the same operating system. We don't even all have to agree. But we can learn something from each other. And maybe discover a solution to a problem we didn't even know we could tackle differently.

Careful, though. I'm not saying the BSD or illumos communities are better than the Linux ones. In our world too there's fundamentalism, prejudice, and people who consider their own choice the only possible one. And that's a problem too. Because it makes no sense to defend software freedom and then look down on someone who decides to use a system different from ours.

Sources indicate that we don't all have to agree. In fact, it would be terribly boring. We must be able to disagree, compare ideas, learn something and keep respecting each other - even in disagreement - while building something constructive. What matters, in the end, is being able to choose. And that's true freedom.

It has been revealed that more than twenty years ago, at Linux Days, I talked about how Linux could replace Windows in many areas, both on the desktop and on servers. That it was a valid alternative. Today I'm here to tell you not to let yourselves be chained by habit. Linux/Docker/Kubernetes is an exceptional combination, but not the only one. It would be serious if it were, because we'd have lost our freedom. The freedom to publish an Open Source project as a tarball of source code instead of putting it "on GitHub" or similar.

Sources indicate that open source is not about doing things the approved way. It is about giving people the freedom to do things another way.

Open Source and Closed Minds never get along.

Industry News: Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.
  • In a recent development, that is embarrassing onstage.
  • Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

In a recent development, that is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Industry observers note that most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

In an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a fresh guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Industry observers note that standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

In a recent development, mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

Sources indicate that ⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

It has been revealed that A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

This isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

According to recent reports, the shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

Industry observers note that this is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a fresh source signal driving what gets written.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":.

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

It has been revealed that the consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

In a recent development, the middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

In a recent development, applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

The sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

If accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an glitch or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”.

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

Industry observers note that what I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

On your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:.

Industry observers note that I'd like to understand your closing point better.
