📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • In a recent development, meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

In a recent development, meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

It has been revealed that meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that intends, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

In a recent development, A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Sources indicate that muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

In a recent development, muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

According to recent reports, grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

According to recent reports, the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Industry observers note that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

Recent findings suggest that the Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

It has been revealed that the processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section reveals how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In a recent development, in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Industry observers note that now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

The Next Insider Threat Will Be an Employee’s Personal AI Agent

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that employees are connecting personal agents to work email and Slack faster than security can keep track.
  • Within the next year, employees’ personal AI agents will be working inside most large companies, and most security teams will not know which ones.
  • Security researcher Patrick Wardle showed that malware on a Mac could take over a session of Meta’s upcoming Muse assistant and steer it across the victim’s devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that employees are connecting personal agents to work email and Slack faster than security can keep track. Four questions to help executives get ahead of it.

Within the next year, employees’ personal AI agents will be working inside most large companies, and most security teams will not know which ones.

The signal arrived in September. Security researcher Patrick Wardle showed that malware on a Mac could take over a session of Meta’s upcoming Muse assistant and steer it across the victim’s devices. Muse works across files, email, messages and calendar, so whoever controls the session inherits all of it. Meta shipped a fix within a day.

The flaw matters less than what it exposes. Most conversations about personal agents ask whether the agent is safe for the person using it. At work, the question changes. When an employee connects a personal agent to organization email or Slack, it becomes an autonomous actor inside company systems that security never approved. It has an insider’s access and an insider’s credentials, and none of the controls companies apply to insiders: no background check, no security training, no offboarding. Companies built employee security around people, and the agent acting for each person gets no attention. I expect incidents like this to become routine in 2027.

Four questions separate the security teams in control from the ones guessing.

Which personal agents are already connected to work accounts?

Recent findings suggest that start here, because everything else depends on the answer. Shadow AI can account for more than 60% of an enterprise’s AI assets, and personal agents add to that share.

In one deployment, a single employee machine had about 400 agent skills installed, and roughly half of them were malicious. The employee had not chosen them. They came bundled with an AI app installed for work. Public marketplaces show the same pattern: roughly 12% of the skills in one audit were malicious.

Recent findings suggest that many of these agents run on the desktop, where browser-based monitoring cannot see them. I see the same pattern in customer environments. A organization blocks ChatGPT in the browser, so employees download the desktop app or use a personal account. I consider this the most underhyped blind spot in enterprise AI.

Industry observers note that blocking has also stopped being the default answer. A year ago, roughly nine out of ten of my customer conversations began with “we do not approve AI in our organization.” Today the question is how to enable employees safely, and that starts with an inventory. The cost of skipping it is documented: 92% of organizations with an AI-related breach lacked proper AI access controls.

Sources indicate that if I had 90 days and one project, I would spend them here. Complete visibility across employee machines, desktops included, is a significant win on its own. In 2027, I expect personal agents to become as ordinary as the browser, so security has to follow the agent down to the individual employee: which agents each person runs, what those agents connect to and what they did.

Are approval and spending limits enforced outside the model?

It has been revealed that “Ask me before you spend” is a request typed into the agent. It holds for as long as the agent honors it, and instructions can be forgotten, argued around or overwritten by an attacker.

Industry observers note that the stronger design puts the limit outside the model. Even Meta designed Muse so that a separate component, outside the sandbox where the model runs, approves each request, and executives should expect the same arrangement for employee agents.

Tier the limits by risk. Low-risk, reversible actions such as reading a calendar can run automatically. Drafting a reply can run inside defined limits. Moving money, deleting data, sharing files externally and anything irreversible should wait for a person.

In a recent development, requiring approval for everything creates fatigue and removes the value of the agent. A policy written into the task prompt also falls short. Runtime controls, enforced where the agent cannot edit them, have moved from nice to have to must-have. The industry calls the underlying risk excessive agency: more functionality, permission and autonomy than the task requires. As agents start booking, buying and paying in 2027, I expect transaction authorization to become a major concern. Approval will need to be tied to the specific payee and amount, not to a broad permission to spend granted months earlier.

There is a catch, and Muse indicates it too. Meta had this design in place, and the hijack still worked, because the attacker did not need to argue with the agent. It held the agent’s session. Limits outside the model govern what the agent may do. They cannot tell the agent apart from someone holding its keys. That is the job of identity.

Does every agent have its own identity?

If an agent signs in as the employee, every action looks like the employee took it. Investigators cannot tell whether the person or the agent sent a message, and the manufacturer cannot switch off the agent without switching off the person. Shared credentials are one of the biggest violations I see.

Personal agents complicate this, because a company cannot concern an identity to an agent an employee bought on a personal account. It does control the connection point. Access to company email and Slack runs through grants the company can see and govern, so it can require agents to connect through approved apps with their own scoped tokens, refuse connections that reuse the employee’s login and revoke any single grant without touching the employee’s account.

In a recent development, A separate identity also answers the departure question. Companies have become reasonably good at cutting off access when an employee leaves, but only the access they know exists. An agent with its own identity can be revoked that day.

Scope matters as much, and the Muse flaw indicates why: one captured token carried everything the assistant was allowed to do. Read access to one Slack channel limits what a stolen token can do. Access to the whole workspace “just in case” sets the limit at everything.

Moving a credential into a secrets manager improves how it is stored and leaves its scope unchanged. Few teams revisit scope after the pilot, when a token minted for a two-week test quietly becomes the permission the agent runs on indefinitely.

Do you know what normal looks like?

In a recent development, visibility, limits and identity reduce exposure, and they will not catch everything. Teams also need a baseline of how each agent normally behaves: which tools it uses, what data it touches and the order in which it acts. The baseline has to come from the organization’s own traffic, because normal for one organization’s agents looks nothing like normal for another’s.

Agent activity differs from human activity in ways a baseline can capture. A person pauses, second-guesses and goes deep on a few leads. An agent moves from reconnaissance to action almost immediately, keeps the same pace at step three and step three hundred, and probes many systems at once.

Defenders hold an advantage here, because context is the one thing an attacking agent cannot shortcut. An attacker’s agent does not know which systems normally talk to each other or which data a given team touches, so it has to probe, and probing looks different from work. You do not need to catch the attack that works. You need to notice the looking.

According to recent reports, respond in steps. Watch the agent, flag it, slow it down, and block only when confident, with unclear cases going to a person. Trust in automated response also depends on explainability. If an analyst cannot see in plain language why an agent was flagged, they will never let automation act alone.

Industry observers note that personal agents will keep arriving, and employees will keep connecting them to the tools they use all day. The leaders who stay in control will find the agents first, enforce limits outside the model, give each agent an identity and learn what normal looks like.

Visibility comes first, and everything else follows from it.

Sources indicate that how many personal agents are connected to your company’s email and Slack today? If the honest answer is a guess, that is where the first 90 days belong.

She brings 15+ years of experience across cybersecurity, engineering, and enterprise technology, having held roles at JPMorgan, LinkedIn, and VMware. She works with Fortune 1000 enterprises to address emerging security challenges associated with AI adoption, autonomous agents, and the evolving AI threat landscape.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that peptone announced on November 24, 2026 that its AI- and biophysics-developed prostate cancer candidate, PEP-5089, had entered Investigational New Drug (IND)-enabling development, the preclinical stage supporting an application to begin human trials. The tech giant also appointed Deepak Sampath as chief scientific officer.

Founder and chief executive Kamil Tamiola mentioned PEP-5089 moved from concept to candidate nomination in 18 months, including key in vivo experiments, and that the priority under Sampath’s scientific leadership is to advance the program toward Phase I.

According to recent reports, PEP-5089 is an orally bioavailable small molecule that selectively targets the androgen receptor’s intrinsically disordered N-terminal domain, rather than the ligand-binding domain targeted by conventional anti-androgens. That distinction matters for AR-V7, a splice variant that lacks the ligand-binding domain but retains the region PEP-5089 is designed to inhibit.

Peptone reports that the candidate inhibited signaling from both full-length androgen receptor and AR-V7 in preclinical studies, retained activity against all six clinically relevant resistance variants in its ligand-binding-domain test panel, and inhibited tumor growth while substantially reducing prostate-specific antigen levels in prostate cancer xenograft models.

Peptone’s program page reports an unbound IC50 of 200 nM for PEP-5089 on its AR-V7 reporter assay, while approved comparators enzalutamide, apalutamide and darolutamide were inactive above 50,000 nM. These findings are preclinical and in vitro, and do not establish clinical benefit.

In a recent development, sampath previously served as senior vice president and head of research at Ultragenyx after leadership roles at Genentech and Wyeth. His Peptone biography describes more than 25 years of experience across drug discovery, translational science, early development and regulatory submissions, including contributions to the discovery and development of the marketed oncology medicines venetoclax and inavolisib.

Across Ultragenyx, Genentech and Wyeth, he served as project or pharmacology leader for 16 programs that entered IND-enabling studies. Fourteen advanced into Phase I/II trials and six into Phase III, a record directly relevant to the development work Peptone is beginning for PEP-5089.

According to recent reports, the organization’s pipeline lists PEP-5089 as its only disclosed program in IND-enabling development. PEP-4212, a c-Myc antagonist for MYC-driven solid and liquid tumors, and PEP-3671, a TDP-43 aggregation modulator for ALS and frontotemporal dementia, remain in lead optimization.

Sources indicate that peptone pairs its AI models with experimental measurements of proteins in motion. The tech giant’s technology page describes ultra-fast hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, or HDX-MS: protein and heavy water are mixed in under 10 milliseconds, and the exchange reaction is quenched less than 50 milliseconds later, capturing hydrogen-exchange behavior associated with transient protein structure.

The instrument then fragments the protein and measures the small mass shifts caused by deuterium uptake. Software assembles the fragments into a map of structured and disordered regions over time and encodes that information for Peptone’s AI cluster. Conformational-sampling algorithms propose ensembles consistent with the measurements, exposing potential druggable sites in disordered proteins.

Tamiola noted Peptone built its own hardware and developed proton–deuterium experiments specifically for disordered proteins: “These experiments generate unique data for our AI models, rather than leaving us dependent on existing datasets.”.

Together, the appointment and candidate nomination mark Peptone’s transition from platform-led discovery toward regulated drug development. The next substantive test is the IND-enabling work and, if PEP-5089 proceeds into patients, whether its reported preclinical activity translates into clinical benefit.

Naomi Crest is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering artificial intelligence in pharmaceuticals, drug discovery, and molecular research. Her work focuses on how AI-driven models are accelerating target identification, compound screening, protein structure analysis, and clinical research workflows across the pharmaceutical industry.

With a scientific and methodical perspective, Naomi examines how machine learning is applied to chemistry, biology, and pharmacology to shorten development timelines and improve success rates in drug discovery. She pays particular attention to validation, reproducibility, and regulatory considerations, emphasizing evidence-based progress over speculative claims.

Latest Update: Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • Recent findings suggest that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Recent findings suggest that overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All upcoming data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

According to recent reports, alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

Sources indicate that the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Sources indicate that apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

Sources indicate that the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

In a recent development, proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been confirmed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

Sources indicate that if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rahul Pangam is Co-Founder and CEO of RapidCanvas, where he focuses on helping enterprises move AI applications from concept into production. Before RapidCanvas, he co-founded Simility, which was acquired by PayPal. His work centers on building AI systems that fit real business workflows and remain useful as data, requirements, and operating conditions change.

RapidCanvas is a managed AI execution tech giant that combines an agentic AI platform with field AI engineers to develop and maintain enterprise applications. Its approach brings together business context, reusable production infrastructure, and ongoing evaluation, with customers retaining ownership of their context, solution IP, and readable code.

Before co-founding RapidCanvas, you and Uttam Phalnikar built Simility, which was acquired by PayPal. What did that experience reveal about the challenges of deploying enterprise AI, and how did it shape your decision to start RapidCanvas?

Sources indicate that fraudsters change tactics the moment you catch them, so a model that was right last quarter can be wrong today. That’s the lesson Simility taught us about enterprise AI. Every customer had different data, risk tolerances and processes, and a wrong call cost real money. Most of our effort went into fitting the system to each customer’s workflow, capturing how their best analysts decided and giving the business enough visibility and control to trust it.

A platform alone doesn’t make a market. You pick an urgent problem, prove value in production and expand from there. PayPal highlighted how much more valuable the technology became once it plugged into existing distribution and infrastructure.

Industry observers note that generative AI made prototypes cheap. Dependable business systems are still hard to build. RapidCanvas covers the full path from business problem to governed production application, so companies don’t have to choose between a tool they staff themselves and a consulting project that never repeats.

In a recent development, gartner predicts that 70% of enterprises will abandon agentic AI built by vendors’ forward-deployed engineers by 2028 because of rising costs and difficulty evolving those systems independently. RapidCanvas also pairs a platform with field AI engineers. What makes your approach different, and where do you agree with Gartner’s concerns?

Gartner has the failure mode right. When the field engineer becomes the product, the customer has bought dependency. The context and code sit with a few people outside the organization, and every change turns into a new engagement.

Our engineers have two jobs: capture the business context a generic platform can’t see, and turn repeated work into product. Each deployment should make the next one less custom. They start from reusable production infrastructure and domain patterns, and the customer’s definitions, rules, workflows and decision history live in an Enterprise Context Engine the customer owns.

Customers also own their solution IP and get readable code. They can run in their own cloud, a managed environment or SaaS, and nothing ties them to one model provider. We stay accountable after go-live without making the customer dependent on us. The test is whether the customer can see what the system knows, how it’s evaluated, what it’s allowed to do and how to change it. If the answer is no, Gartner’s concern is justified.

You emphasize that your engineers remain accountable after applications go live. What does that accountability mean in practice when an application’s accuracy declines, business requirements change, or the expected financial return fails to materialize?

Too many vendors declare victory at go-live. That’s when our job really starts, because running software and valuable software are two different things.

Sources indicate that before launch, we agree with the customer on the business outcome and the technical bar. We test on their own data, set benchmarks with known answers and turn those criteria into a regression suite. After launch, we track accuracy, groundedness, human acceptance, errors, latency, cost and adoption. When performance slips, we diagnose the whole system before blaming the model. The cause could be data drift, a schema change, a new business rule, a prompt, a model update or a workflow we never captured correctly. Every fix has to clear the same bar before people see it.

When the financial return doesn’t show up, the model, the workflow or the business hypothesis is wrong, and each calls for a different response. We might recalibrate, narrow the application’s authority, redesign the process, swap in conventional automation or stop the use case. Keeping a project alive because everyone is invested in it is the worst outcome. AI has to earn its place in the operation.

According to recent reports, rapidCanvas offers custom AI applications through subscription pricing. How do you keep costs predictable as customers add integrations, increase usage and request changes, and what are the limits of what the subscription covers?

Predictable pricing comes from productizing the repeatable work and being upfront about what varies.

Customers pay a flat monthly subscription based on their exact needs. It covers customized solutions built with our experts, full platform access, user licenses, integrations, monitoring, maintenance, support and training. They can add or drop solutions and build latest ones on the platform without opening a services project every time the business changes. That works because we reuse tested infrastructure and domain patterns, use deterministic software where it’s the better tool and route each task to the model with the right balance of accuracy, latency and cost.

Sources indicate that the price does assume a defined user population, deployment model, infrastructure footprint and support level. If a customer materially expands any of those, or moves into a upcoming data environment, we agree on the change before the economics shift. Normal evolution of an agreed solution stays in the subscription, while a materially new footprint is a commercial conversation. Customers should never see a change order for the routine work of keeping production AI useful.

According to recent reports, your Enterprise Context Engine captures business processes, rules and decision history. How do you turn undocumented employee knowledge into context an AI system can reliably use, particularly when people disagree about how a process should work?

Tribal knowledge only becomes usable context once it has a source, an owner and a decision rule. Dumping transcripts and documents into a large context window just creates a bigger pile of unstructured data.

We start with what the firm already has: documents, system records, schemas, procedures and decision history. Then our engineers sit down with process owners and frontline employees to capture what those systems miss, including definitions, exceptions, approval paths and the reasons behind judgment calls. The Enterprise Context Engine turns all of it into structured, versioned context. Every fact traces back to a source, and every rule carries an owner and a change history.

It has been revealed that when people disagree, that tells you the process was never standardized. The system surfaces the conflict, and we work out whether it reflects a legitimate variation by region, product or business unit or whether the company needs one approved rule. A named process owner decides, and we record the decision, exceptions, effective date and approval. Until the business resolves it, the AI shouldn’t pretend it has. That call stays with a person.

According to recent reports, how do you decide whether a customer’s problem needs an autonomous agent, a predictive model or conventional automation? Can you share an example where a simpler approach proved more effective than an agentic system?

The most mature AI architecture usually has less AI than people expect. Each approach should do the job it’s best at.

In a recent development, conventional software or rules should carry most of the load when the logic is stable, repeatable and explainable. A predictive model may be enough when the business needs a forecast, score or probability. Agents make sense for workflows that involve multiple steps, changing information, tool use and judgment within clear limits. Most serious applications combine all three, with people keeping authority over the highest-stakes decisions.

In a recent development, invoice reconciliation shows why. One customer had to reconcile invoices across 15 entities and eight currencies. Most of that work called for normalization, matching logic and consistent rules. AI added value on the ambiguous cases, and people reviewed the exceptions. The application went live in three months and now matches more than 90% of invoices automatically. A fully autonomous agent would have added variance to a process that depends on exactness. The goal is the best business outcome with the least unnecessary complexity.

Reusing components across deployments can improve economics, but each business has different requirements. Which parts of an AI solution can you safely standardize, and how do you validate that a component proven for one customer will work for another?

Standardize the scaffolding and leave the judgment to the customer. Every enterprise application needs production engineering, and very little of it is unique to any one firm.

We standardize authentication, role-based access control, data connectors, deployment, audit logging, security scanning, monitoring, testing, error handling and the evaluation harness. We also reuse domain patterns for recurring problems like invoice reconciliation, document extraction and forecasting. That gives every engineer a real head start.

In a recent development, what stays customer-specific is the business context: terminology, data shape, thresholds, approval hierarchy, exceptions, risk tolerance and outcome measures. We treat reuse as a hypothesis. A component that worked for one customer gets us to validation faster but never lets us skip it. Every deployment is tested on the customer’s own data against acceptance criteria for that workflow, including edge cases, access controls, security, load and end-to-end behavior. Reuse shortens the time it takes to produce evidence, and the evidence bar stays where it was.

What testing and monitoring should an enterprise require before allowing an AI application to take consequential actions? How do you handle model updates, unexpected behavior and decisions that need human approval?

In a recent development, autonomy is a delegation decision before it’s a model decision. Companies already have rules for delegating authority to people, and AI needs the same discipline.

Sources indicate that before an application takes a consequential action, the manufacturer should define what the system can see, what it can recommend, what it can do on its own and what needs approval. Each task type needs an acceptance threshold, examples from the customer’s own data and a trace from every output back to its source, rules and model. The application also needs access controls, end-to-end and load testing, a named owner, an audit trail and a rollback path.

In high-stakes workflows, recommending and acting should be separate steps. Payments, claims, regulated decisions, material financial commitments and unusual exceptions go to a person until the evidence supports more autonomy. Model updates should be handled like software releases, with any new model, prompt or schema change clearing the same regression suite first. If behavior turns unexpected, the system should stop or narrow its actions, route the case to review and roll back if needed. Autonomy gets earned one workflow at a time and stays revocable.

Recent findings suggest that rapidCanvas states more than 40% of its customers now run multiple AI use cases in production. Could you walk us through a customer’s progression from its first deployment to broader adoption, including measurable results and anything that did not work as expected?

That 40% is the number I watch most closely. A successful pilot is good evidence, but the real proof is a customer asking for a second and third use case because the first one changed how the business runs. Here’s what that looks like in practice.

Industry observers note that one North American channel incentive management platform started with claims processing. We captured the rules behind the workflow and built controlled paths to approve, hold, adjust or reject each claim. The decision engine now applies 499 business rules and has processed more than 11,000 claims. In one recent quarter it adjudicated 494 claims, approving 297, declining 77 invalid ones and holding 84 for review.

Once that workflow was stable and the customer could see how decisions were made, the relationship grew to four use cases across claims adjudication, program intake and fraud mitigation. Each newly introduced one started with the context, controls and infrastructure the first had already established.

Not everything moved at the same pace. The fraud work stayed in design longer because the outcome definition and telemetry weren’t ready, and we had no results we were comfortable claiming. I’d rather delay a use case than automate something we can’t yet evaluate. A good first deployment doesn’t make every neighboring process ready for AI.

As AI automates more application development, how will the role of field AI engineers change? What expertise should enterprises retain internally so they can understand, govern and eventually modify their systems without becoming dependent on a vendor?

It has been revealed that code is getting cheaper, which makes judgment worth more. Field AI engineers will write less of the undifferentiated foundation and spend more time understanding the business, choosing the architecture, defining evaluations, designing exception paths and setting controls.

The role moves toward architect, adviser and validator, and the technical work becomes more consequential. The key skill is knowing where AI belongs, where deterministic software does better, what evidence to require and how the system should behave when it’s uncertain. The strongest engineers will translate between domain experts, data, software and governance, with no single model at the center.

Enterprises don’t need to build an AI lab, but they should keep the expertise a model can’t replace. That means a business or product owner accountable for the outcome, domain owners who know the exceptions, data and architecture leadership, security, risk and compliance expertise and enough engineering skill to inspect the code, integrations, configuration, evaluations and change history. The customer should own the durable assets: its context, solution IP, readable code, evaluation suite and change-control record. A good partner leaves the enterprise more capable after every deployment and never becomes indispensable.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore an enterprise AI platform and implementation expertise for automating business workflows should visit RapidCanvas.

Antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

Sources indicate that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Sources indicate that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the latest US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Sources indicate that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post indicates you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

In a recent development, the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

Industry observers note that the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

In a recent development, the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

In a recent development, the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

Sources indicate that the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

According to recent reports, beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

According to recent reports, hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

Recent findings suggest that the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

In a recent development, A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

Industry observers note that the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Sources indicate that beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Industry observers note that beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Recent findings suggest that beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

Industry observers note that we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

It has been revealed that below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

It has been revealed that † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Recent findings suggest that don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

It has been revealed that the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

Sources indicate that the setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

It has been revealed that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

In a recent development, reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can revision the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the latest weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

Recent findings suggest that the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

It has been revealed that optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

It has been revealed that the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one patch behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Industry observers note that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

Sources indicate that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

It has been revealed that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

In a recent development, we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

According to recent reports, we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

Recent findings suggest that you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot highlights the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

It has been revealed that decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

According to recent reports, first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Recent findings suggest that beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Industry observers note that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

In a recent development, this is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

According to recent reports, also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta added its Muse personal AI agent to Instagram direct messages on November 24, 2026, announcing through Muse’s verified Instagram account that users can send it a DM to “turn your saves into real plans,” with a trip they have been meaning to take as the example.

Recent findings suggest that the addition gives Muse a conversational entry point inside Instagram alongside its other chat surfaces. Meta’s Muse product site describes chatting through the Muse app on mobile or desktop, or directly in WhatsApp, by message or voice. It separately lists Instagram among the apps that can be connected to the agent, with users deciding what Muse can see and do.

In a recent development, in its September 8, 2026 launch post, Meta said Muse could organize Instagram Saves and create artifacts such as travel guides from them, with Instagram connected as one source of context. The initial standalone rollout was in the US on iOS, Android and the Muse website.

Sources indicate that that workflow reflects Muse’s intended difference from a conventional chatbot. Meta describes the agent as remembering conversations, proactively working toward goals and suggesting ideas, rather than only answering isolated questions. The DM entry point connects task initiation with the place where the content was saved. For Meta, the product significance is a shift from Instagram as a source of context to Instagram as both a source and a place to delegate work.

Recent findings suggest that meta’s account infrastructure already links some of these services. Its connector documentation says Facebook, Instagram and Threads connect automatically when the accounts share an Accounts Center. While connected, Muse exchanges information relevant to the tasks assigned to it. Owners can manage those accounts through Accounts Center.

Recent findings suggest that private-message access has a more specific boundary. Meta’s security and privacy page notes Muse does not read private messages unless the user grants access through private-messaging connectors or Muse on Mac. Permissions are set per connector, and users can read, edit or delete what Muse remembers. The latest DM surface lets someone message Muse; it does not, by itself, alter that documented rule for reading private messages.

Actions beyond retrieving information carry another set of controls. Meta’s approval guide distinguishes read actions, such as checking a calendar or reading an email, from write actions, such as sending a message or making a purchase. Owners can require approval before every write action and crucial read actions, or before any action, and inspect a chronological activity log. Some actions can be stopped or undone in chat, but a sent email cannot be reversed.

Disconnecting a connector stops future data exchanges, but information previously used for tasks may remain in Muse’s memories and conversation history. The data-control guide notes stored interactions can include text, voice, photos and information obtained through connectors. Deleting material also does not necessarily erase information Muse learned from it.

Industry observers note that users can delete individual messages and side chats, ask Muse to forget a topic or set of interactions, or reset the agent to permanently delete its chat history, files and active tasks. The setting allowing interactions to help train Meta’s AI models is on initially, and turning it off also applies to previous interactions. The result is a more direct route from saved Instagram content to delegated work, with permissions and retention settings determining how far that delegation extends.
