📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Engineering Around Non-Determinism: Evals, Grounding, and Release Gates for AI-Drafted Suspicious Reports.

Nov 24, 2026 12 min read.

Recent findings suggest that financial institutions must investigate potentially suspicious activity and prepare accurate, complete, and timely reports for Financial Intelligence Units. The process is sensitive, labor-intensive, and subject to strict deadlines. This article explains how non-deterministic Artificial Intelligence (AI) components can be incorporated into a dependable agentic system that reduces the cost of doing business, increases drafting and review speed, and maintains the quality of the final report.

A Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) is a formal document submitted by regulated entities and financial institutions to law enforcement or financial intelligence units (such as the UK's National Crime Agency) to flag known or suspected instances of money laundering, fraud, or terrorist financing.

SARs should give a clear and concise explanation of the reason(s) for the suspicion, identifying:.

The Inverted Pyramid Plot Model for SAR narratives organizes information from most to least important, much like a news article.

Because the structure moves from the broadest, most critical information down to the narrowest, a reader can grasp the core of the case from the opening lines alone and turn to the later sections only for supporting detail.

Industry observers note that in the following system context diagram, a human agent views the investigation notes prepared by another human agent and then drafts the suspicious activity report. Once the report is reviewed by another peer, it is submitted to a financial intelligence unit.

System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors).

In the following diagram, there are 4 key timelines of any investigation:.

High-level diagram of a traditional reporting system (Source: authors).

We propose improving the traditional reporting system by using AI to automate selected tasks and generate high-quality SAR drafts, followed by specialized human review and minor edits where necessary. The goal is to increase throughput, reduce cost per case, and decrease reporting failures.

In the following system context diagram, human agent effort is shifted to review/edit the AI-assisted report drafting and review.

System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors).

We changed the earlier design to support background automation of suspicious activity report generation. As soon as the investigation is complete, the case is sent to the queue for processing by the Agentic System. Before the human agent picks the case for drafting the report, the AI Agent has drafted the first version to speed up the report generation.

High-level diagram of an AI-powered reporting system (Source: authors).

The non-deterministic nature of AI, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), creates two central concerns:.

The proposed solution is a multi-agent system, with access to selected LLMs via a gateway, and supported by a tailored knowledge graph built from operational data.

Grounding is the foundation of trustworthy SAR generation. The system should make it easier to state only what the evidence supports, not merely make the prose more fluent.

High-level diagram of the agentic system (Source: authors).

Sequence diagram of Drafter agent, Judge Agent and Human (Source: authors).

Industry observers note that quality means more than well-written prose. It means a complete, internally consistent, reviewable narrative that meets institutional and jurisdictional requirements.

In a recent development, unlike traditional software, LLM outputs are non-deterministic, and "quality" is subjective. In the case of report writing, "what does a good report look like?" becomes more subjective. Hence, there is a need to test the "subjective" aspects against "objective" metrics, and here the Eval shines.

Evals are like tests of regular software development practices, and they can be leveraged in the following processes:.

There are a few broad focus areas where the model output has to be tested on a continuous basis:.

For example, Evals can be written to assess different aspects of the generated narrative like:.

Sample Eval can look like this:.

Industry observers note that once we have scores from all the evals, either we can use a weighted average or a simple average of all the individual scores to figure out the final grading criteria. This is how the Evals can be leveraged to grade the quality of generated output.

Sequence diagram of Evals grading (Source: authors).

According to recent reports, since the model and prompt are bound to change, this adds another dimension of non-determinism to the system. With any production system, we need to have a regression run of all evals against the golden data set before any model upgrade or prompt/config change happens.

According to recent reports, the golden data set has to be collected initially with different edge cases with defined input and output. This will help in testing the system during development. The Golden Data Set can be augmented with human feedback in production where they love the output generated by the AI system.

Evals shall answer some of the generated report’s quality metrics like :.

In a recent development, traditional testing is a deterministic process of verification - it asks, "Did we build the product right?" against a fixed specification. This approach fails when a system’s core logic is probabilistic, because non-deterministic output may be more likely to introduce subtle degradations of quality that do not result in explicit crashes and may not be repeatable. Hence, it is crucial to monitor the decision-making trajectory, from initial intent to final outcome.

The system is gradually improved by generating telemetry, understanding the system, and patching the underlying challenges.

Human review remains a policy decision owned by the BSA/AML function. AI accelerates preparation; it does not replace accountable judgment.

In a recent development, treat models and prompts as regulated production changes. The release plane provides controlled progress rather than "ship and hope.".

The bottleneck in drafting a quality Suspicious Activity Report was qualified personnel. LLM-based systems can reduce that dependency, but only if they're engineered for it, with grounding and evals as the substitute for the judgment of a qualified investigator.

The mechanism we've described treats non-determinism as an engineering problem rather than an excuse. Grounding drafts in a case-specific knowledge graph and operational data keeps the Drafter Agent grounded in evidence. A Judge Agent and deterministic fact-checker turn "does this read well?" into measurable checks against factuality, completeness, and the Inverted Pyramid structure the FIU expects. Evals and a golden dataset give these subjective judgments an objective, regression-testable backbone, the same way unit tests do for deterministic code. And a release process that versions models, prompts, and configuration, gated with shadow/canary rollout and feature-flag rollback, treats every change to the system as a production release.

Recent findings suggest that none of this shifts accountability away from the humans who own it. The BSA/AML officer still decides what gets filed; the agentic system's job is to make sure that when a human reviews a draft, the evidence is already assembled, the uncertain claims are flagged, and the reviewer's time goes to judgment rather than transcription. Risk-tiered routing means the system earns trust on familiar, low-risk cases before it is ever allowed near the ones that matter most.

SAR narratives can now be drafted at machine speed, by codifying what "good" looks like into evals a machine can check against. When a human reviews the output, they're not taking the narrative on faith; they can trace the reasoning and the evidence lineage behind it, and that traceability is what turns speed into trust.

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that torchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • According to recent reports, torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that torchNeuron provides a upcoming native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

According to recent reports, torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a upcoming backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

Industry observers note that to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron customers use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Sources indicate that text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

According to recent reports, now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Recent findings suggest that parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

It has been revealed that the command below introduces training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

It has been revealed that many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

It has been revealed that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Sources indicate that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, consumers can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google unveiled on November 24, 2026 that its Workspace Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and Workspace command-line interface (CLI) are generally available, alongside rules requiring AI agents to use those interfaces instead of existing REST APIs.
  • Google reports that Workspace APIs handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, with public Drive API traffic more than two-and-a-half times its 2022 volume.
  • Google’s rationale is that traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced applications, where a valid OAuth token implied user intent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google unveiled on November 24, 2026 that its Workspace Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and Workspace command-line interface (CLI) are generally available, alongside rules requiring AI agents to use those interfaces instead of existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins February 1, 2027.

Google reports that Workspace APIs handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, with public Drive API traffic more than two-and-a-half times its 2022 volume. Traditional applications can continue using existing REST APIs; the new requirement applies to AI agents and other AI-driven tools.

Google’s rationale is that traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced applications, where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. An autonomous agent acting at machine speed across email, documents and cloud infrastructure changes that assumption. The fresh design puts policy checks, data boundaries and human confirmation into the request path.

The Workspace servers use MCP to give AI applications a standard way to read data and take actions. Dedicated remote servers are generally available for Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat and Tasks, inheriting each user’s permissions and data-governance controls. The Workspace CLI serves local agents, terminal workflows and automation, with structured JSON output and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services.

Each agent call through these interfaces is checked against organizational permissions, data-loss-prevention rules and classification labels. The MCP servers reject OAuth clients that are not designated for AI agents, and agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs with least-privilege scopes and usage quotas. Billing is scheduled to begin on April 1, 2027, while time-limited approvals are listed as coming soon.

In a recent development, draft creation and document summarization can run autonomously. Sending email, changing Drive sharing permissions and making bulk edits require explicit user confirmation. Workspace administrators can view, audit and revoke agents in the admin console; user-facing activity review and revocation, plus controls to block agent access to Gmail messages and specific Drive files or folders, remain forthcoming.

The Workspace AI Tools Addendum covers standalone agents, the software harnesses that deploy or orchestrate them, and applications or services using AI models. It bars disguising a tool to avoid classification or circumvent the Google MCP requirement. That makes the migration a compliance issue for third-party agent platforms as well as for developers building directly on Workspace.

Recent findings suggest that workspace user data and Google Technical Information, a category of service information obtained or derived through Workspace access points, may be processed only to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks. Neither category can be used for model training, fine-tuning, evaluation dataset construction, model distillation or developing a service similar to a Workspace service. Scraping and systematic probing beyond what an authorized task requires are also prohibited.

Google Technical Information cannot be stored for more than 30 days. Covered user data and technical information must not be retained after a tool is disconnected or its access is revoked. If Google reasonably believes those rules have been violated, it can immediately restrict or remove the tool’s access, or suspend or terminate the customer’s access to the relevant Workspace services.

In a recent development, on Google Cloud, Agent Gateway verifies Agent Identities against the Agent Registry directory, enforces identity and access management policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor. It governs inbound client-to-agent traffic and outbound requests from agents to tools, APIs and other agents. Custom authorization checks can be delegated to an organization’s own policy engine or third-party security tools through Service Extensions.

Recent findings suggest that cloud Run support and Agent Gateway for cross-cloud Kubernetes environments remain in Limited Preview. Each gateway instance can govern up to 5,000 resources registered in Agent Registry.

According to recent reports, google’s MCP configuration guide requires screening prompts and responses for indirect prompt injection, meaning hidden instructions in untrusted content, using Model Armor or a documented alternative. Malicious emails or documents could hijack a session and modify, steal or delete data. Current known problems include some English-only approval prompts, no user self-service viewing or revocation of saved tool approvals, and expiration of those approvals after 90 days.

Sources indicate that for enterprises, agent governance is now built into the supported Workspace access path. The practical burden is the migration: existing agent integrations must satisfy the upcoming identity, confirmation, screening and retention rules on Google’s schedule, while parts of the user-control and deployment model remain pending.

Breaking: Leash Biosciences Raises $11M to Build Scientific AI Training Worlds

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leash Biosciences unveiled an $11 million financing on November 24, 2026 to build scientific AI training environments from wet-lab measurements.
  • Innovation Endeavors reported that Leash’s collection has reached 6.3 million molecules, 44 billion experimental measurements and more than 1,200 proteins.
  • The financing follows Leash’s October 14, 2026 introduction of Minos, a framework that turns premeasured protein–small-molecule binding experiments into replayable worlds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leash Biosciences unveiled an $11 million financing on November 24, 2026 to build scientific AI training environments from wet-lab measurements. Innovation Endeavors invested alongside Insight Partners, backing Leash’s effort to give AI agents reusable experience from physical experiments.

Innovation Endeavors reported that Leash’s collection has reached 6.3 million molecules, 44 billion experimental measurements and more than 1,200 proteins. The investor’s thesis is that AI for medicine development needs more and better data, not simply larger models and more compute, and that Leash’s measured datasets can address models’ difficulty generalizing beyond their training data.

The financing follows Leash’s October 14, 2026 introduction of Minos, a framework that turns premeasured protein–small-molecule binding experiments into replayable worlds. An agent selects experiments within a constrained budget, receives outcomes derived from wet-lab measurements rather than human or model judgments, updates its hypotheses and chooses again. The physical work is paid for during construction, allowing subsequent agent runs to reuse the measurements at computational speed.

An accompanying working draft calls this property counterfactual density: researchers can compare an agent’s choices with the measured outcomes of alternatives it skipped. Historical datasets contain only experiments their original creators chose to run, while conventional lab-in-the-loop systems must physically run additional experiments to obtain newly introduced outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that in the main cold-start task, an agent must find the strongest binder it can among roughly 1 million or 6 million molecules, depending on the library, with no starting hits and a budget of 100 molecule tests submitted in batches of up to five. This is a simplified structure-activity relationship campaign, meaning the agent uses measured responses to chemical changes to guide subsequent choices.

Sources indicate that leash tested 58 combinations of chemical library, model and inference effort. The draft reports substantial variation in performance: greater inference effort generally helped within model families, but spending alone did not determine success. Many configurations outperformed random search.

To test whether agents were using chemistry, researchers scrambled the molecular structures associated with building-block identities while preserving those identities and the measured outcomes. Performance dropped sharply in both libraries, which Leash interpreted as evidence that agents were using chemistry information rather than relying solely on structure-blind local search.

In a recent development, leash also examined 4,602 independent structure-activity-relationship trajectories and identified recurring failure modes: stopping before the experimental budget was exhausted, repeatedly testing the same molecule and weaker models persevering in unproductive chemical neighborhoods. Stronger models more often abandoned those neighborhoods, showing how the environments can expose decision processes rather than just endpoint scores.

The STRELKA release contains Minos worlds for 34 protein targets screened against AMA020, packaged for Harbor, together with narrations from that trajectory corpus. The official STRELKA page asks visitors to request access.

The experiments remain narrower than full medicinal chemistry. They concern binding enrichment against single protein targets, not the broader optimization of potency, selectivity and drug-like properties required in development campaigns. Agents are also restricted to molecules already screened unless Leash orders or synthesizes and tests new ones.

The financing backs a data infrastructure approach in which the value lies in reusable physical experience, not just the binding candidates a screen might produce. Leash’s working draft leaves open whether experience acquired in Minos improves scientific decision-making in previously unseen physical worlds, a central qualification for its potential use in reinforcement learning and other post-training.

#92351. Industry News: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

Industry News: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and upcoming Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

According to recent reports, you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

In a recent development, you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each newly introduced token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Sources indicate that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Industry observers note that the decoding kernel indicates up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Industry observers note that working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Recent findings suggest that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Sources indicate that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

According to recent reports, audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them latest paths through Metal:.

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Sources indicate that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

According to recent reports, work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

It has been revealed that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

Sources indicate that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

In a recent development, bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

According to recent reports, pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A significant thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

Epochal Debuts Time Portal to Test Forecasting AI on Web History

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Epochal, a latest AI manufacturer, introduced itself on November 24, 2026 with Time Portal, a point-in-time web environment for AI agents.
  • In a recent development, the unveiled team includes Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss, key members of xAI’s founding team, alongside Alex Bocharoff and Frank Luan.
  • According to recent reports, the company’s premise is that today’s models absorb the internet with many outcomes already visible, whereas people learn by making decisions before knowing the results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Epochal, a latest AI manufacturer, introduced itself on November 24, 2026 with Time Portal, a point-in-time web environment for AI agents. The company notes the archive spans more than 1 trillion pages and is designed to teach systems to forecast without exposing future outcomes.

In a recent development, the unveiled team includes Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss, key members of xAI’s founding team, alongside Alex Bocharoff and Frank Luan. Time Portal, Epochal’s first product, was built in 90 days.

According to recent reports, the company’s premise is that today’s models absorb the internet with many outcomes already visible, whereas people learn by making decisions before knowing the results. Epochal wants agents to rehearse that process across thousands of historical days, using the web as it existed at each selected moment rather than as a single training corpus filled with hindsight.

Epochal reports that Time Portal tracks more than 7 trillion URLs across over 30 years of internet history, with minute-level version granularity on the most dynamic pages. Its three components have distinct jobs: search finds historically available pages, fetch retrieves a specific URL, and sandbox supplies a Linux environment gated to the same instant.

The sandbox addresses ways an agent could notice the simulation without reading a future page. Its system clock is set to the chosen instant, while the Ubuntu version, system libraries, language runtimes and command-line tools match that period. Package mirrors and network requests also respect the cutoff, placing commands and web browsing inside the same historical environment.

It has been revealed that to assess how closely the simulation matches live deployment, Epochal ran forecasting agents on 347 live questions from prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket. A few weeks later, it replayed those questions through Time Portal with each cutoff set to the original forecast time. Separate replays gave agents either the live web or no web access.

In a recent development, in Epochal’s own evaluation, the correlation between Time Portal replay errors and original live forecast errors was 0.98, compared with 0.16 for live-web replays after resolution and 0.49 without web access. The Time Portal replays revealed no significant deviations in predictions from the historical runs. Live-web agents could look up resolved outcomes, reducing errors to nearly zero, while no-web errors were larger and only loosely tracked the originals. The experiment therefore measures historical fidelity: how closely a replay matches the original run.

An engineering post describes a strict retrieval rule: fetch returns the newest capture at or before the requested instant and returns a miss if none exists. A later snapshot is never substituted because even the closest future copy could reveal information that was unavailable at the time. The engine also marks disappeared pages as absent, collapses duplicate content within and across URLs, and adjusts ranking as the meanings of terms and facts change.

Recent findings suggest that developers can start with a limited version for free through the API, console playground or SDKs. The API documentation notes the playground does not require an API key, while API calls use an Epochal key and an Accept-Datetime header containing a past timestamp. Python and Rust clients, a command-line interface and an MCP server are also provided. When a sandbox stops, its filesystem and command output are discarded.

For Epochal, Time Portal is infrastructure for a broader effort to train AI through decisions and observed outcomes rather than static historical text. Its archive and strict cutoffs address how forecasting experiments can be staged without hindsight. Whether work in these reconstructed pasts produces better predictions on unresolved events is the central question for the company’s approach.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

In a recent development, the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Industry observers note that reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the upcoming provider can't replay them.

Industry observers note that API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Recent findings suggest that while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

Recent findings suggest that and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

According to recent reports, community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

In a recent development, language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

The research — most notably from Thomas Stanley and William Danko's landmark study "The Millionaire Next Door" and Chris Hogan's follow-up study of over 10,000 millionaires — consistently shows that the typical American millionaire is a middle-aged person with a modest lifestyle who has been saving and investing for 25-30 years.

This matters for the FI community because it proves that building a million-dollar net worth is not about luck, inheritance, or extraordinary income. In a recent development, for FI purposes, investable assets are the more meaningful measure — your home equity does not fund your retirement spending unless you sell or downsize. But by either measure, the US has more millionaires than any other country in the world.

Industry observers note that note: Growth includes both new wealth creation and inflation. A million dollars in 2000 had the purchasing power of approximately $1.8 million in 2024 dollars.

The average millionaire started investing at age 29 and became a millionaire at 49. They are your neighbors, not the people on magazine covers.

The research paints a consistent picture of the typical American millionaire — and it looks very different from what pop culture suggests.

Recent findings suggest that every FI practitioner is building toward a net worth that exceeds $1 million. The data from "The Millionaire Next Door" and subsequent research validates the FI approach completely: live below your means, invest the difference in diversified low-cost funds, avoid debt, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting over 15-25 years. InfoQ Homepage Presentations Inferencing for Enterprises.

Dio Rettori discusses the operational realities of enterprise AI inference. Moving beyond fast token generation, he explores why inference requires dedicated systems engineering, tackles GPU utilization pitfalls, compares on-prem versus cloud TCO, and analyzes multi-agent latency determinism. He shares why teams must embed domain ontology directly into models rather than relying solely on RAG.

Dio Rettori leads Product for Global AI Infrastructure Platforms at JPMorganChase, bringing 25+ years of experience. He previously oversaw the firm's multi-cloud strategy and led cloud transformation for Asset & Wealth Management, modernizing apps and driving cloud adoption at scale. Earlier, he held product and marketing leadership roles at Red Hat, Pivotal, and Solo.io in cloud-native solutions.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Interhuman AI Tests How Models Read Social Signals Beyond the Transcript

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pause in conversation can signal hesitation, uncertainty, or simply that someone is thinking.
  • Sources indicate that the research preprint describes a video track with ten signals, including interest, skepticism, and confusion, and an audio track with six.
  • It has been revealed that in a conventional exact-label score, confusing hesitation with uncertainty is simply an error.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pause in conversation can signal hesitation, uncertainty, or simply that someone is thinking. A transcript may not record the pause at all. Interhuman AI’s Social Signal Bench, publicized on November 24, asks AI models to identify observable signals like these from video and audio, then scores them against the judgments of trained human raters. Its most useful feature is how it handles an awkward problem: two trained observers can watch the same clip and reasonably come away with different labels.

Sources indicate that the research preprint describes a video track with ten signals, including interest, skepticism, and confusion, and an audio track with six. A model can predict more than one signal in a clip. The held-out test sets contain 2,372 video clips and 1,094 audio clips. Interhuman has made the dataset card and training data publicly available, while keeping the expert-labeled test material separate for hosted evaluation.

It has been revealed that in a conventional exact-label score, confusing hesitation with uncertainty is simply an error. So is confusing hesitation with agreement. Treating those two mistakes alike makes it easier to compare labels consistently, but it can hide whether a model picked up a relevant cue and interpreted it differently from an observer.

In a recent development, interhuman’s alternative, Evidence-Weighted F1, gives partial credit for related labels and gives more weight to a signal backed by stronger annotation evidence. Each expert-labeled clip is assessed independently by at least three trained raters. Their labels capture when a behavior was visible or audible, how strong it appeared, and how certain the observer was about the label. Agreement among raters is useful, but disagreement isn’t automatically discarded. If observers had different reasonable readings, the scoring method can retain evidence for each.

Sources indicate that that does not mean a model can earn an easy score by listing everything it might have seen. The benchmark pairs predictions with reference labels one to one and penalizes unmatched predictions. The choice of how closely different labels are related still comes from the authors’ taxonomy. A different definition of which mistakes matter most could change what a good score looks like, which is one reason exact-label scores remain useful alongside the upcoming metric.

The benchmark fits into Interhuman’s broader work on models that process conversations as audio and video. The company’s technical write-up describes outputs that include a predicted signal, a confidence level, and a short account of the evidence. A keyword search would miss an example like a speaker agreeing verbally while slowing down or pausing; the benchmark asks whether models can recognize behavioral cues rather than rely solely on the literal words.

But the human labels reflect what observers perceived. They cannot establish whether a speaker really felt uncertain or why they paused. Culture, speaking style, the setting, and the short length of the clips all affect interpretation. The public dataset is primarily English online video with one clearly visible speaker; the held-out sets broaden that selection but do not establish that results transfer to every language, community, or interaction. The dataset terms also rule out unconsented surveillance and high-stakes uses such as hiring or workplace monitoring.

According to recent reports, the immediate value is a better way to test how multimodal models respond to ambiguous evidence, particularly when a system might otherwise treat a transcript as the entire conversation. It also clarifies what a high score cannot tell us: a model may be good at matching trained observers on selected clips without reliably knowing what a person intended. That gap is precisely what makes a carefully bounded benchmark useful.

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • Industry observers note that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • According to recent reports, TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

Industry observers note that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

According to recent reports, TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch consumers had to work harder to get in.

According to recent reports, until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

According to recent reports, torchTPU adds TPU as a latest backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

It has been revealed that transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

It has been revealed that the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Industry observers note that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Recent findings suggest that models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

In a recent development, we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

Recent findings suggest that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It has been revealed that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an concern on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 complications, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • According to recent reports, this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

According to recent reports, this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

In a recent development, the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Upcoming Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

Recent findings suggest that the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

Industry observers note that the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

In a recent development, call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table demonstrates that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table reveals which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In a recent development, in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

Industry observers note that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

According to recent reports, in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

According to recent reports, replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

Recent findings suggest that with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

Industry observers note that key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

Recent findings suggest that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A video generator asked to follow reference footage can spend a surprising share of its time revisiting details that barely change: an empty sky, a flat wall, or a stretch of road.
  • Recent findings suggest that the distinction matters for anyone evaluating faster video generation.
  • Reference-guided generation lets a creator provide more than a prompt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A video generator asked to follow reference footage can spend a surprising share of its time revisiting details that barely change: an empty sky, a flat wall, or a stretch of road. In a release on November 24, Anorak mentioned its AI lab had developed a way to cut that repeated work. The method improved end-to-end generation speed by about 1.5 to 1.6 times on two benchmarks in the team’s research preprint, without retraining the underlying model. A separate result that exceeded twice the original speed combined the method with another optimization.

Recent findings suggest that the distinction matters for anyone evaluating faster video generation. The authors measured one model, a version of MiniMax-H3 already optimized with eight denoising timesteps and 8-bit quantization. The findings suggest there was still meaningful room to reduce computation in an already streamlined system. They do not show that the method halves generation time across video models or makes them responsive enough for live interaction.

Reference-guided generation lets a creator provide more than a prompt. An image can supply the appearance of a character, while a rough animation can show the motion or composition a finished clip should follow. In the architecture studied by the researchers, the model represents those references as tokens and examines them alongside the tokens for the output it is generating. Reference tokens account for roughly half of that combined sequence in the configuration described in the paper. Longer sequences are expensive because full attention compares tokens with one another; the number of those comparisons grows roughly with the square of sequence length.

Yet not every part of a reference contributes equally. A patch of sky that barely changes from frame to frame adds less new information than a moving subject. There is an important exception: a static detail can still be central to what the creator asked for. A logo on a moving car may be visually repetitive across the reference but essential to the shot.

Anorak calls its method PCRG, short for pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation. It uses two signals the system already produces. The first indicates whether the compressed visual information is repetitive. The second, drawn from the part of the system that reads the visual inputs and prompt together, helps identify which pieces of the reference are relevant to the output.

According to recent reports, the method keeps processing tokens that add distinctive information. It processes repetitive but relevant tokens once, then reuses part of that computation as the clip is refined. It drops repetitive tokens that the system identifies as less relevant before those refinement passes start. Instead of asking the model to do fewer rounds of refinement, the method reduces how much reference information it has to reconsider in each round. That difference explains why it can be combined with some other speedups.

The researchers reported a 1.57× end-to-end speedup on their V2V-Bench test suite and 1.49× on the public VACE-Benchmark. Their VBench quality measure declined by 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. Combining PCRG with Veda reached 2.15× on V2V-Bench. These are author-reported results, and a small change in an aggregate score cannot rule out errors in an individual clip.

Recent findings suggest that for Anorak, the research is part of a broader effort to make generated footage respond to players. Workflows that repeatedly adjust a reference or generate alternative takes could benefit even if the technology falls short of real-time play. How far the gains extend is an open question: a workflow with short or little reference material has less redundant input to remove, and a model that handles references differently may not see the same improvement. The next useful evidence would be a comparison across more model families and longer, more varied inputs, with timings and visual quality reported together.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the features are built around the open Model Context Protocol (MCP) and its extension system, allowing supporting servers to work in compatible clients beyond Claude.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic declared on November 24, 2026 that Skills over MCP is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code, while Tasks and Elicitation are generally available and File Uploads will roll out soon. The additions let connected servers supply workflow guidance, run lengthy jobs, request user input and, once File Uploads arrives, exchange files with Claude.

Recent findings suggest that the features are built around the open Model Context Protocol (MCP) and its extension system, allowing supporting servers to work in compatible clients beyond Claude. Anthropic reports more than 700 million monthly MCP SDK downloads and over 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude, describing the ecosystem it is asking to implement the latest server capabilities.

According to recent reports, tool names and descriptions tell Claude what a server can do; skills add guidance on how to handle particular use cases. A server can publish best practices, step-by-step workflows or playbooks tailored to a user’s account or organization alongside its tools. Claude retrieves a skill only when needed, and updates arrive with the server, so users do not install anything separately.

Recent findings suggest that the Skills extension documentation defines a skill as a directory containing a SKILL.md file and optional supporting files, with discovery and retrieval handled through MCP’s existing Resources primitive. Hosts may not fetch files ahead of need. Before use, they must verify each file’s byte size and SHA-256 digest and compare the instruction file’s frontmatter with the approved manifest; changed files require fresh approval. SDK and host support across clients is still being implemented.

The beta is on by default for Pro, Max and Ultra looks, available to Team plans after an administrator enables it, and listed as coming soon to Enterprise. Anthropic’s examples include Shopify for designing and updating online stores, HubSpot for customer onboarding and Atlassian for organization-specific analysis. A forthcoming Carta skill is intended to draft and matter equity from an uploaded document.

Tasks and Elicitation are available to Pro, Max and Ultra prepares in Claude and Claude Code and are rolling out to Team and Enterprise organizations. Tasks lets a server run a time-consuming operation or a full agent loop in the background while Claude continues other work and retrieves the result later. ZoomInfo uses it for deeper account and contact research that previously required several prompts.

Industry observers note that the Tasks documentation indicates the server returns a durable task handle instead of blocking the connection. Clients can poll for progress and resume with the same task ID after a disconnect or restart. States cover working, input required, completion, failure and cancellation, and a task can request input before proceeding. Cancellation is cooperative, so the server acknowledges the request without being obligated to stop the underlying work.

It has been revealed that elicitation lets a server pause for user input through a form or link before continuing. Supabase uses it to confirm paid-project costs and destructive SQL, Railway to ask before potentially destructive changes, and GitHub to request a repository name before deletion. The Elicitation specification separates structured form input from URL-based interactions and bars servers from using forms to request passwords, API keys, access tokens or payment credentials. Clients must identify the requesting server and provide decline and cancel options.

In a recent development, anthropic prepares File Uploads for Claude and Claude Code on Pro, Max, Ultra and eligible Team and Enterprise plans. It will allow PDFs, spreadsheets and images to pass to MCP servers without going through the model’s context window.

Industry observers note that the File Uploads repository makes its earlier-stage status explicit: the extension is experimental, is not part of the MCP specification and has not been proposed for inclusion, so breaking changes are expected. Its design keeps file bytes out of model context and JSON-RPC messages. A server marks file arguments, the client uploads missing bytes and retries, and a tool can return a download target in result metadata.

In a recent development, anthropic also reports that on-demand tool search can reduce the context used by tool definitions by more than 85% in multi-server setups. That efficiency focus connects the separate additions: skills load only when needed, tasks avoid holding a connection open, and file transfers are designed to keep bytes out of model context. The result is a broader coordination layer for agent work, whose reach depends on servers and clients implementing the same extensions and on the file-transfer design stabilizing.

Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2188 w)
