General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • Recent findings suggest that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

Recent findings suggest that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

It has been revealed that the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Industry observers note that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

According to recent reports, the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

Industry observers note that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Industry observers note that think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

Sources indicate that they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping tech giant: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

In a recent development, third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

Recent findings suggest that to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

Industry observers note that vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Industry observers note that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cognition released SWE-2.1 on November 24, 2026, reporting a Terminal-Bench 4.1 score of 50.0, up from 24.2 for SWE-2. Alongside the base model are a Cerebras-backed Lightning variant and SWE-2.1 Cyber, a more permissive version rolling out to Devin Security.

It has been revealed that like SWE-2, the newly introduced model was trained with pure reinforcement learning on Kimi K3. Cognition attributes much of its coding improvement to targeting general intelligence and long-horizon workflows; its FrontierCode 2.0 score reached 41.3, compared with 24.1 for SWE-2. The same table puts Claude Opus 5.5 at 47.3 on FrontierCode and 65.8 on Terminal-Bench, leaving SWE-2.1 behind that model on both tests despite its gains over SWE-2.

According to recent reports, cognition expanded its training tasks and environments across short- and long-horizon workflows, spanning software engineering, science, performance engineering and cybersecurity. New post-training algorithms control rollout length during training. The company notes reducing length oscillations stabilized training on tasks lasting from a few minutes to many hours, while performance on held-out evaluation tasks improved steadily over many days.

That recipe also changed how the model uses additional computation during a run. On ExploitGym, Cognition reports a log-linear increase in cumulative solve rate as normalized rollout time lengthens, with a steeper test-time-scaling curve than the base model. In practical terms, the model continued finding exploits as runs extended for hours. The chart normalizes speed with a fixed tokens-per-second rate, one second of time to first token and actual tool-execution time, so the sustained-run results reflect a simulated time budget rather than raw serving latency.

Sources indicate that cybersecurity is central to the release. Cognition reports 80% on ExploitBench, up from 36.1% for SWE-2, and a 27.3% ExploitGym success rate for intended exploits, up from 12.1%. Its broader flag-capture rate reached 44.8%, compared with 18.1%; that metric also counts successful real exploits unrelated to the vulnerability specified in the initial prompt. The results cover both vulnerability discovery and completion of full exploitation chains, often during several hours of autonomous work.

Those capabilities also changed the training-security requirements. Cognition red-teamed its training setup, especially its sandboxes, added continuous safety monitoring and built a canary evaluation that alerts researchers after a successful sandbox escape. The model discovered upcoming sandbox vulnerabilities four times during training despite that red-teaming; Cognition says researchers were alerted and responded immediately each time.

The deployed model adds safeguards aimed at a narrow set of high-harm activities, which Cognition claims are calibrated to leave most legitimate work, including cyber defense, unaffected. Because some defensive tasks require restricted capabilities, SWE-2.1 Cyber will use more permissive safeguards in Devin Security. It will power normal scans, while existing deep scans use frontier cybersecurity models such as Mythos, pairing a less restricted defensive model for normal scans with the established deep-scan option.

Sources indicate that cognition’s demonstration demonstrates SWE-2.1 Lightning generating 600 tokens per second, compared with 60 for standard SWE-2.1 and 200 for SWE-2 Flash. The Cerebras partnership provides the same model at 10 times the standard rate, which matters because the model continues improving with additional test-time compute: higher throughput increases how much investigation and iteration can fit into an urgent fix or active incident. Lightning is free through December 8, 2026, and available in Devin Desktop, Cloud and CLI at a discounted price.

The benchmark numbers also depend on Cognition’s evaluation choices. It uses upstream or self-reported scores when available and otherwise tests models internally, with closed models in their developers’ preferred harnesses and open and SWE models in Devin CLI. ExploitGym uses pass@1, meaning one evaluated attempt, over 869 tasks with a six-hour timeout and mitigations disabled, while ExploitBench combines captured flags from five runs per task under a three-hour simulated clock. The release’s practical significance therefore rests on two connected questions: whether the longer-horizon gains hold outside these evaluation settings, and how much Lightning’s additional throughput converts them into completed engineering and defensive work under real deadlines.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Mentioned It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

Sources indicate that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

According to recent reports, figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Industry observers note that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

It has been revealed that we call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

Recent findings suggest that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Recent findings suggest that table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

Sources indicate that what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but tech giant policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a recent development, in a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

Recent findings suggest that in our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

Recent findings suggest that if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 reveals which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

Sources indicate that the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

According to recent reports, table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

Sources indicate that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

According to recent reports, the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

It has been revealed that table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Industry observers note that figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

Industry observers note that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Industry observers note that figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Sources indicate that selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Sources indicate that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

Sources indicate that for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each upgrade generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Industry observers note that zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

It has been revealed that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

Industry observers note that no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

Recent findings suggest that thinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

It has been revealed that A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Industry observers note that each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Sources indicate that figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Sources indicate that figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

Industry observers note that when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Sources indicate that nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

According to recent reports, when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

Recent findings suggest that in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google DeepMind on November 24, 2026 launched Humanity’s First Exam on Kaggle, a benchmark of 544 elementary text and image prompts designed to test whether large language models answer routine questions consistently, not just correctly once.

Sources indicate that the accompanying technical report evaluated 18 frontier and fast-tier models. Its primary measure, family pass^4, estimates the probability that all 16 sampled attempts across four related prompts are correct; family pass@4 instead asks whether at least one of those attempts succeeds.

According to recent reports, the report ranks GPT-6.2 Astra first at 92.4% family pass^4, followed by GPT-6.2 Sol at 86.9% and Gemini 4 Neon at 85.8%, although all three reached 100% family pass@4. The report calls the difference the Family Reliability Gap: 7.6, 13.1 and 14.2 percentage points, respectively. That difference matters for automated work in which an occasional correct answer is insufficient.

Recent findings suggest that the 544 prompts form 136 families, each containing a seed and three controlled variants that preserve the underlying task while changing entities, clause order or visual attributes. The 20 subcategories include object counting, color identification, spatial reasoning, arithmetic, constraint satisfaction and false-premise verification. Of the total, 316 prompts combine text and images, while 228 are text-only.

Sources indicate that one public example asks for the colors, in order, of the third letter of each word in a neon sign. The reference answer is green, yellow, white, blue, blue. Such tasks are deliberately easy to explain, while their variants test whether a correct answer depends on a particular phrasing or image.

Researchers evaluated the models zero-shot in a single turn without external tools, drawing six independent answers per prompt and grading the visible final answer with a deterministic Gemini 3.1 Pro judge. The analysis found that among the top 12 models, 61% to 85% of families with any failed rollout had just one problematic prompt while the other three were solved on all six runs.

The report’s failure analysis attributes 73% of wrong-answer rollouts to visual perception, including 31% involving position, direction or paths in images and 23% involving object counting. Among the top nine models, family pass^4 ranged from 83% to 97% on text-only families but fell to 64% to 89% on multimodal families.

Recent findings suggest that the report’s reasoning-effort tests show that moving Gemini 4 Carbon from low to high effort raised family pass^4 by 17.4 percentage points overall, with a 42.4-point gain on Math and Algorithmic tasks versus 3.1 points on Vision tasks. The pattern indicates that additional test-time computation can catch symbolic and procedural slips while leaving visual-perception and variant-robustness failures largely unresolved.

The report’s screening process began with 315 complete five-prompt families. The researchers retained only families whose seed was solved by at least three of four independent human raters, audited ambiguity and variant fidelity, and standardized each surviving family to four prompts. Single-rater human accuracy on the 136 retained seeds was 90.8%. Raters could not use LLMs, web search, calculators, code or writing assistants.

It has been revealed that only 112 prompts in 28 families are public under CC-BY-4.0; another 432 prompts in 108 families remain private to reduce contamination and overfitting. The Kaggle benchmark uses an isolated evaluation environment without public internet access and a 16-model leaderboard. It separately documents configuration and sampling differences from the paper’s 18-model evaluation, so their scores should not be treated as equivalent runs.

According to recent reports, the authors caution that tasks were adversarially selected to expose model blind spots rather than sampled uniformly from everyday queries, and list synthetic imagery, reliance on one Gemini autorater family and seed-only human testing as further limitations. HFE therefore functions as a stress test of elementary reliability; its scores do not estimate how often models will fail across ordinary use.

It has been revealed that google DeepMind is also inviting submissions through a three-week Kaggle competition ending December 15, 2026, asking for everyday questions that current models still answer incorrectly so HFE can be refreshed. The central deployment question is whether a system can reproduce an elementary success on every call, particularly when small wording changes or basic image interpretation can break it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

Recent findings suggest that the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

It has been revealed that to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

According to recent reports, select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script releases its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

In a recent development, each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel initiative use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS indicates nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space indicates comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

According to recent reports, each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando.
  • Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.
  • OpenAI has detailed Pando, a newly introduced backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

OpenAI has detailed Pando, a newly introduced backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches.

Recent findings suggest that pando now powers all development in OpenAI's monorepo and is serving nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. OpenAI attributes the increased load to Codex-driven development, and each push can in turn trigger multiple CI jobs that all fetch the same history. Pando went into production in April 2026.

Rather than replace Git's client and protocol, OpenAI has changed how the backend coordinates reference updates and stores and transfers objects. On a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it's being streamed to immutable blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. A metadata transaction records the reference version (containing the fresh branch tip, the packfile and its dependencies on earlier reference versions) and atomically updates the reference pointer. Updates to unrelated references can proceed independently of one another; updates to the same reference still need to be coordinated.

Sources indicate that openAI refers to this as causal consistency with serialisable updates to individual references and read-your-own-write consistency. A reader gets the history needed for the requested revision, but fetching a number of branches won't provide a repository-wide snapshot. Two clients can see different combinations of branch versions during concurrent updates. The trade-off removes a shared coordination point for unrelated pushes.

Pando also changes how Git decides which objects to transfer. By default, when a client pushes a new feature branch, the server will advertise only a designated trunk branch as its base. That constrains the dependencies of the resulting packfile, which in turn allows Pando to reuse it for readers who already have that trunk history. Repeated or stacked branch pushes can resend objects outside trunk, trading some additional bandwidth for the benefit of reusable packs.

Pando’s topic-branch packs depend on advertised trunk history and can repeat objects from earlier pushes (source).

Sources indicate that for fetches, Pando maps the client's existing and requested commits to reference versions and picks out the appropriate stored packs to cover the missing history. Git's packfile-uri capability allows the server to return download links rather than generate a bespoke pack for each client. Express, a regional pack-delivery cache, serves those downloads. OpenAI reports cache-hit rates in excess of 99% and tests in which clone and fetch operations saturated 10 Gbps network links.

Industry observers note that background compaction groups packs into larger, geometrically sized covers, resembling compaction in a log-structured merge-tree. The covers provide better compression and act as a skip-list-like index for fetch planning. Pando keeps packs at every level so that clients with different histories can still be served.

Pando groups successive packs into larger covers to improve compression and fetch planning, retaining packs at every level (source).

Sources indicate that the design contrasts with Anthropic's Scion, previously covered by InfoQ. Scion replaces Git's underlying model with changesets recording files changed relative to their first parent and content-addressed pointers to compressed file contents; commits, merges, rebases and history queries run server-side. Its clients retrieve missing immutable trees and blobs, rather than negotiate Git packfiles, and use bounded local caches and sparse or virtualised checkouts.

Both systems make use of immutable data and regional caches to reduce repeated computation. The way in which they draw the compatibility line is very different, though. Pando preserves Git's object model and client-side workflows and changes the backend coordination and delivery. Scion, on the other hand, assumes an online client and moves the repository operations into a dedicated service. The improvements they report are not directly comparable. OpenAI reports on push latency, whereas Anthropic reports on checkout speedups and infrastructure reductions compared with its previous Git-based setup.

According to recent reports, git compatibility did not eliminate migration work. OpenAI initially deployed Pando as a read- and write-through proxy, moved clients in phases, and migrated hundreds of integrations using legacy APIs, webhooks and repository downloads. It also distributed its own Git build, which supports parallel downloading and indexing of independent packs. OpenAI indicates some client improvements are already upstream, with others available in its public repository.

Industry observers note that for the architects, it's a case of two separate decisions: which source control operations go on the server and which of the consistency and transfer guarantees do the workloads actually need. Pando retains the Git workflows but dispenses with the repository-wide snapshot across branches and accepts redundant transfers in order to reduce the amount of coordination and per-fetch computation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that anthropic announced on November 24, 2026 that Claude users can install artifacts as desktop apps in beta on macOS and Windows. The apps have their own windows and icons, are rolling out to free and paid looks, and can request access to files, programs, notifications, and other operating-system features.

Sources indicate that artifacts are Claude-generated designs, documents, dashboards, and small interactive tools that open beside a conversation for editing and sharing. A user describes the desired tool in chat, and Claude writes the code. Tools that call Claude run on Anthropic’s infrastructure without API keys; each person signs in with their own Claude account and gets a separate instance, with usage counted against that person’s plan rather than the builder’s.

Sources indicate that the beta is rolling out on Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise looks and requires Claude for Mac or Claude for Windows version 6.28899.0 or later. A user opens the artifact in Claude Desktop, selects Install as app from its title menu, context menu, or sharing options, and confirms. macOS places apps in a Claude Apps folder, while Windows apps can be opened from the Start menu or a desktop shortcut.

Industry observers note that installation adds a desktop container without creating an independent copy: the app remains the same artifact. Edits by the owner or another editor therefore change the app, and opening it requires an internet connection and a signed-in Claude Desktop session. An app with a menu bar item or system tray icon keeps running after its window closes.

According to recent reports, installed apps retain the artifact’s access to Claude and connectors. They can also request permission to show notifications, respond to keyboard shortcuts while other apps are in use, float over other windows and read cursor position, and display a macOS menu bar item or Windows system tray icon. A separate full-access tier can run programs and read, change, or delete files without repeated prompts. The installation guide warns that Anthropic does not review apps before installation and advises granting full access only when the user trusts everyone who wrote the app.

It has been revealed that claude generally prevents full-access requests if someone outside the user’s organization wrote part of the app or authorship cannot be confirmed. On Free, Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, anyone other than the user counts as outside. Permission is version-specific: allowing one version does not cover an patch, even when the user made the edit, while a refusal remains until changed. Code loaded from another site can change without triggering a latest request.

Sources indicate that team prepares enable installation by default but leave full computer access off until an admin enables it. Enterprise plans keep the entire feature off until an owner turns it on. Building an app and any requests it makes to Claude count toward the user’s proposal limits.

At launch, installation is unavailable on Linux, the web, and mobile. Artifacts made from templates, including Docs, Slides, and Sheets, cannot be installed, nor can legacy artifacts or live artifacts from Claude Cowork. Organizations with HIPAA-ready configurations cannot use the apps. Full access is unavailable in Claude for Teachers and K-12 organizations, and installed apps are not covered by zero data retention in organizations using it for Claude Code.

Sources indicate that the change gives a conversational request a route to software that sits beside other desktop programs, but it also brings code authorship, file access, retention, and administrative policy into that route. The result is an app-distribution model whose identity, updates, usage, and controls remain tied to Claude and the underlying artifact.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • Industry observers note that LFM2 revealed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

Industry observers note that LFM2 revealed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

According to recent reports, the payoff highlights at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

In a recent development, every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two newly introduced in-house encoders:.

In a recent development, each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Industry observers note that reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Industry observers note that reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a fresh in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

According to recent reports, reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

According to recent reports, we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

Ambarella and Liquid AI announced a strategic collaboration on November 24, 2026 to run agentic AI directly on devices that interact with the physical world, pairing Liquid’s foundation models with Ambarella’s low-power CVflow edge architecture.

Industry observers note that liquid foundation models are now available in the Cooper Model Garden within Ambarella’s Developer Zone, allowing developers to build applications with the models running directly on Ambarella silicon. Support for more Liquid models is planned across the CV72, CV75 and N1-655 systems-on-chip (SoCs) and the X7 AI accelerator. That wider hardware support remains a blueprint rather than current availability.

The joint engineering work initially focuses on LFM3, introduced in October 2026, and its execution on Ambarella’s CVflow AI architecture. Ambarella’s edge AI SoCs combine CVflow processing with image-processing and video capabilities, while Liquid supplies the foundation models. The companies stated the optimization is intended to reduce AI compute and memory utilization, producing a smaller DRAM footprint and lower system power for multimodal vision-language and agentic AI workloads.

Sources indicate that the companies connect that memory focus to constrained DRAM supply and rising memory prices across the electronics industry. Lower memory requirements could reduce reliance on expensive configurations and create system-level cost advantages as on-device intelligence expands.

According to recent reports, liquid’s contribution extends beyond models to an agent harness, the software infrastructure used to deploy and operate autonomous agents. Together, the models and harness are designed to let agents repeatedly interpret information, reason about their environment, select actions and verify outcomes. The combined stack is intended to move physical AI systems beyond perception and inference while keeping that loop local, without continuous cloud connectivity.

Recent findings suggest that through its co-design approach, Liquid works with enterprise customers to optimize the models and harness for particular applications and hardware platforms, allowing systems to combine multimodal perception, contextual understanding, reasoning and action while maintaining awareness over time. Running these capabilities locally can improve responsiveness, privacy and operational resilience while reducing reliance on cloud inference, according to Liquid.

Liquid AI Head of Business Erika Wool described the device constraint: “Intelligence must operate where data is generated, with the ability to perceive, reason, remember, and act within the power, memory and latency constraints of real-world devices.”.

In a recent development, the companies are initially targeting intelligent security and smart infrastructure, where systems must interpret complex visual and contextual information, understand changing conditions, make autonomous decisions and respond in real time. They plan to demonstrate solutions built with LFM3 models on Ambarella SoCs at CES 2027.

The immediate deliverable is developer access through Cooper; wider model support across the hardware portfolio and the CES demonstrations remain future milestones. The collaboration’s practical test is whether lower compute and memory use can sustain multimodal agents that maintain awareness over time within device memory, power and cost budgets, without depending on continuous cloud connectivity.

#92315. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that language models can do a lot.
  • Say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they mentioned (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's newly introduced speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

It has been revealed that parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

In a recent development, qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

According to recent reports, the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

In a recent development, we measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Industry observers note that parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's upcoming is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

It has been revealed that urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

According to recent reports, emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

It has been revealed that the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

It has been revealed that the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

According to recent reports, reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Sources indicate that raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

According to recent reports, language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Recent findings suggest that like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Recent findings suggest that each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.
